How to beat this exam

  • She told you what she grades, in her presentation rubric: setting & historical context → characters & plot → theme with quotations → literary devices & dramatic form. Build every long answer in that order.
  • Her own handouts (the Renaissance intro, the Britannica article, the Shakespeare and sonnets sheet) are now three context units in Intel: the Renaissance, the theatre, and Early Modern English. Short answers will come straight out of them: dates, definitions, ‘why did X matter?’.
  • Learn 3–4 short quotations per play. Her rubric asks for ‘at least three key quotations’. Short exact lines beat long wrong ones.
  • The course description keeps saying Turks, Moors, Ottoman Empire, cultural encounter. Any essay that can mention Bajazeth or ‘Soliman and Perseda’ should.
  • Short answers: define → example from a text → why it matters, in 3–5 sentences.
  • Doctor Faustus is taught Nov 4, a week before the exam. Read it before class, not after.
  • Compare whenever you can (overreacher vs revenger, Petrarchan vs anti-Petrarchan). ‘Compare with his contemporaries’ is a learning outcome.

Shakespeare // Intel

W1–2The English Renaissance: rebirth, print and a nervous golden age

Her handouts in one breath: after the Dark Ages and the Black Death, Europe turns optimistic, prints books, reads the Greeks and Romans and decides humans can be perfected. England arrives late, grabs everything at once, and has its greatest century under enormous strain. Britannica calls it a doubleness: new possibilities and new doubts at the same time.

What the Renaissance was (her intro handout)

  • Renaissance = rebirth: an awakening after the ‘Dark Ages’, and a deliberate break with feudal life. Landowners lose their grip as the cities grow.
  • Humanism: Greek and Roman philosophy and myth as inspiration; the belief that humans can reach earthly perfection. The mood is optimism, with the Black Death still a fresh memory.
  • Threads across Europe: nationalism, the first stirrings of democracy, a rising middle class, booming trade, ideas travelling with goods (Venice → Paris → London). Young English aristocrats start ‘touring’ the Continent.
  • England before this was seen as a cultural wilderness; even English was looked down on. Thomas More wrote Utopia in Latin.
  • The English Renaissance: 1500–1660 in her intro (the Britannica article says 1550–1660). Late compared with Italy (14th century), but its literature rivals anything in Europe.
  • Dominant forms: poetry and drama. Poetic genres (lyric, elegy, pastoral…) have strict conventions for style, subject and occasion; verse is often set to music; the aim is beauty and truth in words.
  • English writers love mixing genres: Spenser's The Faerie Queene blends romance, tragedy, epic and pastoral. Milton's Paradise Lost closes the period.

Timeline

YearEvent
1534Act of Supremacy: Henry VIII breaks with Rome. England becomes Protestant (on and off).
1558–1603Elizabeth I. 1559 religious settlement; excommunicated by the Pope in 1570.
1564Shakespeare and Marlowe both born.
1571Battle of Lepanto: the Holy League defeats the Ottoman fleet.
1576James Burbage builds The Theatre, the first purpose-built London playhouse.
1580–81Ottoman trade privileges for English merchants; the Turkey Company (later the Levant Company, 1592). Elizabeth corresponds with Sultan Murad III.
1587The Rose opens (Philip Henslowe). Mary Queen of Scots executed. Tamburlaine on stage.
1588Defeat of the Spanish Armada. Anti-Spanish, anti-Catholic mood.
1592–94Plague closes the theatres. The Spanish Tragedy printed (1592).
1593Kyd arrested; Marlowe stabbed to death in Deptford.
1599The Globe built on Bankside.
1603James I; the Lord Chamberlain's Men become the King's Men.

The printing press

  • Gutenberg's press with fast movable type (her handout: around 1440; the language page says c. 1450). Cheap, quick copies.
  • Results: literacy rises; the Reformation spreads (Luther's 95 Theses); literature stops being a privilege. The democratisation of the written word.
  • Reading itself changes: from one text read aloud to a group (and the oral tradition) to silent, individual reading, which people first found odd and even suspicious. The lone reader interpreting a text is the Renaissance image.
  • In England: William Caxton starts printing in 1476. The first book printed in English is his translation The Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye (printed in Bruges, 1473–74). His best sellers: Chaucer's Canterbury Tales and Malory's tales of King Arthur.

Elizabethan and Jacobean (the Britannica article)

  • Elizabethan: Elizabeth I, 1558–1603. Jacobean: James I (James VI of Scotland), 1603–1625. Together, ‘the most brilliant century’ of English literature.
  • The doubleness: radiant, confident and heroic, but also a time of traumatic strain. The conditions that made the Renaissance possible were already falling apart. New possibilities plus new doubts = the literature's intensity.
  • Society: population doubles; prices and rents rocket; real wages hit bottom in the 1620s; merchants and ambitious gentry rise at the expense of aristocrats and labourers. Behind the fashion for pastoral poetry: sheep farmers enclosing land. Vagrancy and crime are the great unsolved problem (King Lear).
  • New science: Copernicus' sun-centred universe unsettles everything. Donne, The First Anniversary (1611): the new discoveries leave the old world ‘spent’.
  • Religion: the Tudor church is an instrument of political control; the Elizabethan settlement is a compromise attacked by Puritans and Catholics alike. Calvinism tells writers they are corrupt and can't earn salvation, so Jacobean tragic heroes are victims of divine purposes that are terrifying yet inscrutable. (Hello, Faustus.)
  • The race to catch up: Erasmian humanist schooling (Colet, Elyot) to produce officials; Italian models: Petrarch's sonnet, Ariosto's epic, Sannazaro's pastoral, blank verse; Castiglione's The Courtier (Hoby's translation, 1561): wit, sprezzatura (effortless-looking accomplishment), Neoplatonic love of beauty as the path to virtue.
  • Machiavelli: The Prince (1513) had no English translation until 1640, attacked in public and read in private. Bacon thanked him for describing what men do, not what they ought to do.
  • Humanist dignity vs Calvinist helplessness: Seneca-style faith in human constancy against the idea that man can do nothing. Elizabeth held these tensions together; under the Stuarts they fly apart.

Ideas in the air

  • Humanism: classical learning, human potential, the individual (Erasmus, More). Faustus is a humanist scholar gone wrong.
  • Reformation theology: Calvinist predestination (are some people damned in advance?). Central to Faustus.
  • The Great Chain of Being: a fixed hierarchy from God to stones. Tamburlaine, a shepherd who becomes emperor, smashes it.
  • Machiavelli (The Prince): read in England as a manual of cunning evil. The stage ‘Machiavel’ is born: Lorenzo in Kyd.
  • Seneca: Roman tragedy as the model: five acts, ghosts, revenge, long rhetorical speeches, horror.
  • The Turk: feared (Ottoman expansion, Lepanto, Malta) and admired (wealth, power), and a trading partner. ‘To turn Turk’ meant to convert to Islam, or simply to betray.

Court, patrons, and why it ended

  • The court steers the arts. Courtiers protect themselves with double meanings and sly wit, and that verbal fencing goes straight into the poetry and drama (Shakespeare's characters talk like courtiers).
  • Patronage: wealthy nobles fund artists; works are dedicated to patrons, sometimes the same work to several hopeful ones. Most writers still needed another job. (Her handout: four hundred years have changed little.)
  • No copyright: writers didn't own their words, one reason authorship (even Shakespeare's) is hard to pin down.
  • The end (her handout): optimism turns to decadence and cynicism; Puritanism brakes the arts; Elizabeth leaves no heir, and political uncertainty follows. The theatres close in 1642.

What they’ll askHer handouts are short-answer gold: ‘What does Renaissance mean?’, ‘What is humanism?’, ‘Why was the printing press important?’, ‘Elizabethan vs Jacobean?’, ‘Why did the English Renaissance end?’ Define → one fact → why it matters. For essays, open with two sentences of context (Reformation, Armada, Ottoman encounter, the ‘doubleness’).
W1–2The theatre: from morality plays to the Globe

How theatre went from a village-fair attraction to the focal point of the age, who hated it, and who wrote for it.

From festival to industry

  • Middle Ages: touring actors perform morality plays, ‘live-action sermons’, for country audiences.
  • 1567: the Red Lion, one of the first commercial playhouses, just outside London. 1576: The Theatre (James Burbage), the first purpose-built London playhouse. About 20 theatres in the next 70 years.
  • Britannica: the theatre was the focal point of the age. Tickets were cheap; apprentices, fishwives and labourers stood in the yard, and the same play could be staged at court that night. A mixed audience = multiple perspectives on every issue.
  • The stage offered something rare: a literary career that actually paid, so the most skilled writers came to it.

Three traditions feeding the stage (Britannica)

  • Humanist / classical: court, universities, the Inns of Court. Seneca as the model (chorus, ghosts, formal verse; ten Seneca tragedies translated in 1581). Gorboduc (1561, Sackville and Norton): a political warning for Elizabeth and the earliest known English play in blank verse.
  • Popular / native: touring, country festivals, morality plays. The Vice, the tricky villain of the morality play, lives on in Richard III; the clown steps out of the play to joke with the audience. Cambises (c. 1560): a blood-and-thunder tyrant play.
  • Court revels and masques: boy companies; later the hugely expensive court masques for James I and Charles I, written by Ben Jonson and designed by Inigo Jones.

The playhouses

  • Open-air amphitheatres (The Theatre, Curtain, Rose, Swan, Globe) in the suburbs and on Bankside, outside the City's control.
  • Thrust stage with the audience on three sides; groundlings standing in the yard for a penny; galleries for richer people. Daylight performances.
  • Little scenery, rich costumes; a trapdoor (hell, graves) and the ‘heavens’ above. All women's roles played by boy actors.
  • Companies protected by noble patrons: the Admiral's Men (Henslowe and the star Edward Alleyn, who played Tamburlaine and Faustus); the Lord Chamberlain's Men (Burbage, Shakespeare).
  • Plays licensed by the Master of the Revels. Puritan enemies of theatre (Stephen Gosson, The School of Abuse, 1579).

Its enemies

  • Locals hated the crowds, the noise, and the pubs and brothels that sprang up nearby. Critics said plays made apprentices skip work and children skip school, and that the subjects were wicked.
  • Above all the Puritans: they feared that cross-dressing (boys playing women) and play-acting would spread sexual corruption. (Stephen Gosson, The School of Abuse, 1579.) They win in 1642.

Playwrights

  • University Wits: Marlowe, Greene, Peele, Lyly, Nashe, Lodge. University-educated men writing for the commercial stage. Kyd wasn't a university man but worked in the same world.
  • Marlowe's ‘mighty line’ (Ben Jonson's phrase): blank verse (unrhymed iambic pentameter) made the standard voice of tragedy.
  • Kyd (1558–94): Merchant Taylors' School; arrested in 1593 when ‘heretical’ papers were found, which he said belonged to Marlowe, his former room-mate. Died 1594.
  • Marlowe (1564–93): shoemaker's son from Canterbury, Cambridge scholar, probably a government agent, accused of atheism, killed in Deptford by Ingram Frizer.
  • Britannica on the University Wits: the name shows social pretensions, but their drama was middle class, patriotic and romantic: history mixed with clowning, music and love. Peele (The Arraignment of Paris, to flatter Elizabeth), Greene (comical histories: Friar Bacon and Friar Bungay), Lyly (courtly comedies for the boy actors: Gallathea, Endimion).
  • Britannica on Marlowe: the only one who saw the tragic potential of the popular style. Heroes of towering ambition speaking in ‘high astounding terms’; damned in his day as an atheist, homosexual and libertine; his verse makes us sympathise with gigantic villain-heroes.
What they’ll askShort-answer favourites: ‘What was the Red Lion / The Theatre?’, ‘Why did the Puritans hate the stage?’, ‘Who were the University Wits?’, ‘Why is Gorboduc important?’, ‘What is blank verse?’, ‘What is a Machiavel?’.
W1–2Early Modern English: the language of Shakespeare

An ELT topic hiding in a literature course: between 1500 and 1650 English grabs thousands of new words, printing starts to fix its spelling, its vowels move, and Shakespeare bends the grammar for fun.

A word explosion

  • Early Modern English (16th–18th c.) is one of English's great word-making peaks, sometimes called its Golden Age. 1500–1650: about 10,000–12,000 new words, roughly half still in use.
  • English wasn't considered precise or serious enough for scholarship: More, Newton and Harvey wrote in Latin; Gibbon even wrote in French first. Francis Bacon wrote in both and coined words from Greek (thermometer, pneumonia, skeleton, encyclopaedia). Newton's Opticks (1704), in English, brought lens and refraction.
  • Nationalism gradually pushed the native language into intellectual life instead of Latin.
  • Renaissance borrowing was deliberate, not the result of invasion. It peaked around 1600, mostly from Latin (and Greek, some French), often through translations of classical works: kept intact (genius, species, radius, focus, apparatus, nausea) or adapted (horrid, pathetic, pungent, frugal, anonymous).

The Great Vowel Shift

  • A big change in pronunciation in the 15th–17th centuries: long vowels moved higher and further forward in the mouth; short vowels mostly stayed.
  • It separates Middle from Modern English: you can read Chaucer with effort, but his pronunciation would be almost unintelligible; Shakespeare's would just sound accented.

Printing and standard spelling

  • Caxton brings the press to England in 1476 (Gutenberg's was c. 1450 in Germany). Up to 20,000 books in the next 150 years; cheaper books → literacy → English books outsell Latin ones.
  • Before that: five dialect areas: Northern, West Midlands, East Midlands (down to London), Southern, Kentish. Church had about 30 spellings, she 60, though around 500.
  • Southern -eth (goeth) vs northern -s (goes): the northern ending won.

Shakespeare's language

  • He exploited English's flexibility, turning nouns into verbs (‘verbification’): ‘he pageants us’, ‘it out-herods Herod’, ‘uncle me no uncle’, ‘Lord Angelo dukes it well’.
  • A vocabulary of about 34,000 words and about 2,000 neologisms: barefaced, critical, leapfrog, majestic, obscene, gnarled, assassination, courtship, eyeballs, lonely, gloomy, hurry… Her handout's caveat: many simply appear first in his works; he also used other people's coinages and dialect words.
  • Phrases still in use: one fell swoop, vanish into thin air, brave new world, in my mind's eye, laughing stock, star-crossed lovers, there's the rub, it's Greek to me, brevity is the soul of wit, cold comfort, cruel only to be kind, fool's paradise, flesh and blood.

Words from trade

  • Naval power and world trade bring loanwords from everywhere: French (ballet, chocolate, passport), Italian (carnival, balcony, opera, umbrella), Spanish (armada, cannibal), Dutch (yacht, landscape, boss), Arabic (algebra, alcohol, magazine), Persian (bazaar, caravan).
  • Turkish: coffee, yoghurt, caviar, horde, chess, kiosk, tulip, turban. Ottoman trade again: same story as the Levant Company and the Turk on stage.
What they’ll askShort answer on Shakespeare's language or the Renaissance and English: 10–12k new words, deliberate Latin borrowing, the Great Vowel Shift, Caxton and standard spelling, verbification with one example, about 2,000 coinages (with her caveat).
W3Shakespeare's Sonnets 18, 60, 130

Two sonnets saying ‘my poetry will beat Time’ (18, 60) and one saying ‘my poetry won't lie like everyone else's’ (130). Know the form, the turn, and two lines from each.

Form and context

  • Shakespearean (English) sonnet: 14 lines of iambic pentameter, three quatrains + a couplet, rhyming ABAB CDCD EFEF GG. The volta (turn) often comes at line 9 and/or in the couplet.
  • Petrarchan (Italian) sonnet: octave + sestet (ABBAABBA CDECDE). Petrarch's lady Laura set the conventions: golden hair, eyes like suns, cruel beauty.
  • Published 1609 by Thomas Thorpe, dedicated to the mysterious ‘Mr. W. H.’ 154 sonnets: 1–126 to the Fair Youth (1–17 urge him to have children), 127–152 to the Dark Lady.

Shakespeare: her handout's biography

  • Baptised 26 April 1564 in Stratford-upon-Avon; died 23 April 1616. ‘The Bard of Avon’, England's national poet.
  • A member of the Lord Chamberlain's Men from about 1594: actor, playwright and shareholder. The Globe went up in 1599 on the south bank of the Thames.
  • 37 plays, c. 1590–1613. Early: histories (Henry VI, Richard II, Henry V: weak or corrupt rulers, often read as justifying the Tudors; Julius Caesar echoing fears about Elizabeth's lack of an heir) and comedies (A Midsummer Night's Dream, Much Ado, As You Like It, Twelfth Night). After 1600: the great tragedies (Hamlet, Othello, King Lear, Macbeth). Last: tragicomedies (Cymbeline, The Winter's Tale, The Tempest) that end in reconciliation.
  • 1605: he bought Stratford property leases for £440 that paid £60 a year. An entrepreneur too, which bought him time to write.
  • His life is mostly a mystery (only the works and official records). His reputation as a genius peaked with the Romantics and Victorians.

The sonnet craze (Britannica)

  • Sidney's Astrophel and Stella (written 1582, published 1591) starts a vogue for sonnet sequences: Daniel's Delia (1592), Drayton's Idea's Mirror (1594), *Spenser's Amoretti (1595, unusually about love fulfilled in marriage), and Shakespeare's (1609*).
  • The English form (three quatrains + couplet) turns Petrarch's contemplative sonnet into an argument that ends with an epigrammatic sting.
  • Britannica on Shakespeare's sonnets: the conventions are turned upside down: the lady is no beauty but dark and treacherous, and the beloved is male. His irony and dramatic toughness ‘explode’ the form's limits.
  • Keats' phrase for Shakespeare: negative capability: every attitude finds itself in his work, and is questioned there too.

Sonnet 18 “Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?”

  • Q1–Q2: summer is worse than the beloved: too windy (‘rough winds’), too short (‘too short a date’), too hot, and every beauty fades by chance or nature.
  • Volta, line 9: ‘But thy eternal summer shall not fade’. The beloved won't fade because he lives in the poem (‘eternal lines’).
  • Couplet: as long as people breathe and read, ‘this’ (the poem) lives and gives life to you.
  • Themes: poetic immortality, time vs beauty. Devices: extended metaphor, rhetorical question, personified Death bragging, a pun on ‘lines’ (verse lines and lines of time).
  • Irony: the poem ends up praising itself more than the youth.

Sonnet 60 “Like as the waves make towards the pebbled shore”

  • Q1: our minutes rush to their end like waves to a beach, each pushing the one before.
  • Q2: a life from birth (‘Nativity’) to maturity, then ‘crooked eclipses’ attack its glory; Time destroys what it gave.
  • Q3: Time pierces youth's beauty, digs wrinkles in beauty's brow, and mows everything with his scythe.
  • Couplet: yet my verse will stand into the future, praising you despite Time's cruel hand.
  • Note: sonnet 60, about minutes. Devices: simile of waves, personified Time with scythe, astronomical and farming imagery.

Sonnet 130 “My mistress' eyes are nothing like the sun”

  • An anti-Petrarchan blazon (a blazon lists the lady's body parts with fancy comparisons). Every comparison is denied: eyes not like the sun, lips less red than coral, breasts dun not snow-white, hair like black wires, no roses in her cheeks, her breath ‘reeks’, her voice is less pleasing than music, and she walks on the ground like a normal woman.
  • Couplet: yet my love is as rare as any woman misrepresented with ‘false compare’.
  • Themes: honest love vs poetic cliché; satire of Petrarchism; the Dark Lady (dark beauty against the fair ideal). Devices: parody, negation, comic plain diction (‘reeks’, ‘wires’).

Connections

  • 18 and 60: art defeats Time. 130: art should tell the truth. 18 makes a grand comparison; 130 mocks comparison itself.
  • Pure Petrarchan hyperbole in Marlowe: Faustus' ‘Was this the face that launched a thousand ships’. Great contrast with 130.

The three poems (her handout's texts)

PartLines
18 · Q1Shall I compare thee to a summer's day? / Thou art more lovely and more temperate: / Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May, / And summer's lease hath all too short a date:
18 · Q2Sometime too hot the eye of heaven shines, / And often is his gold complexion dimm'd; / And every fair from fair sometime declines, / By chance or nature's changing course untrimm'd;
18 · Q3But thy eternal summer shall not fade / Nor lose possession of that fair thou owest; / Nor shall Death brag thou wander'st in his shade, / When in eternal lines to time thou growest:
18 · coupletSo long as men can breathe or eyes can see, / So long lives this, and this gives life to thee.
60 · Q1Like as the waves make towards the pebbled shore, / So do our minutes hasten to their end; / Each changing place with that which goes before, / In sequent toil all forwards do contend.
60 · Q2Nativity, once in the main of light, / Crawls to maturity, wherewith being crown'd, / Crooked eclipses 'gainst his glory fight, / And Time that gave doth now his gift confound.
60 · Q3Time doth transfix the flourish set on youth / And delves the parallels in beauty's brow, / Feeds on the rarities of nature's truth, / And nothing stands but for his scythe to mow:
60 · coupletAnd yet to times in hope my verse shall stand, / Praising thy worth, despite his cruel hand.
130 · Q1My mistress' eyes are nothing like the sun; / Coral is far more red than her lips' red; / If snow be white, why then her breasts are dun; / If hairs be wires, black wires grow on her head.
130 · Q2I have seen roses damask'd, red and white, / But no such roses see I in her cheeks; / And in some perfumes is there more delight / Than in the breath that from my mistress reeks.
130 · Q3I love to hear her speak, yet well I know / That music hath a far more pleasing sound; / I grant I never saw a goddess go; / My mistress, when she walks, treads on the ground:
130 · coupletAnd yet, by heaven, I think my love as rare / As any she belied with false compare.

What they’ll askShort answer: identify the sonnet from a line, give the rhyme scheme, locate the volta. Long answer: ‘Time and poetic immortality in Sonnets 18 and 60’ or ‘Sonnet 130 and the Petrarchan tradition’.
W4Thomas Kyd, The Spanish Tragedy

The play that invented English revenge tragedy. A father who is also a judge can't get justice for his murdered son, goes half mad, and takes revenge through a play-within-a-play. Hamlet is basically its son.

Basics

  • Thomas Kyd; date uncertain (syllabus: 1582; often placed c. 1587); printed 1592. A huge hit, revived and expanded (the 1602 ‘additions’).
  • Setting: the courts of Spain and Portugal after a war Spain has won. Catholic Spain on stage just after the Armada: the audience is primed to see corruption.
  • Frame: the Ghost of Andrea and the figure of Revenge sit on stage and watch the whole play as a chorus.

Who's who

  • Andrea: dead Spanish courtier, killed in battle by Balthazar. His ghost wants revenge.
  • Revenge: allegorical figure; promises Andrea that Bel-imperia will kill Balthazar.
  • Hieronimo: Knight Marshal of Spain, a judge. Father of Horatio. The revenger.
  • Isabella: Hieronimo's wife; goes mad with grief and kills herself.
  • Horatio: their son; captures Balthazar in battle; loves Bel-imperia; murdered.
  • Bel-imperia: Andrea's lover, then Horatio's. Sister of Lorenzo. A strong, active woman who drives the revenge.
  • Lorenzo: her brother; the Machiavel villain who plots everything.
  • Balthazar: Portuguese prince, prisoner in Spain, wants Bel-imperia.
  • Pedringano: Bel-imperia's servant, bribed by Lorenzo. Serberine: Balthazar's servant.
  • King of Spain, Duke of Castile (Lorenzo's father), Viceroy of Portugal (Balthazar's father).

Plot by act

  • Act 1: Andrea's ghost tells his story; Revenge promises satisfaction. Horatio and Lorenzo both claim to have captured Balthazar; the King splits the honour. Bel-imperia turns to Horatio, partly to revenge Andrea.
  • Act 2: Pedringano betrays the lovers' secret meeting. In the arbour, Lorenzo, Balthazar and their servants hang Horatio and stab him. Hieronimo wakes and finds his son's body.
  • Act 3: Bel-imperia's letter written in blood names the killers; Hieronimo suspects a trap. Lorenzo covers his tracks: Pedringano kills Serberine, then is hanged, joking to the end because he thinks a boy's box holds his pardon. It's empty. Pedringano's letter confirms Lorenzo's guilt. Lorenzo blocks Hieronimo from the King. Hieronimo, half mad, weighs Christian patience against revenge in the ‘Vindicta mihi’ soliloquy and chooses secret revenge.
  • Act 4: Isabella cuts down the arbour and kills herself. Hieronimo stages a play for the royal wedding: ‘Soliman and Perseda’, a tragedy at the Turkish court, acted in ‘sundry languages’. The killings are real: Hieronimo kills Lorenzo; Bel-imperia stabs Balthazar, then herself. Hieronimo shows Horatio's corpse, refuses to explain further, bites out his tongue, stabs the Duke of Castile and then himself with a penknife.
  • Epilogue: Andrea's ghost assigns his friends to bliss and his enemies to eternal torments.

Themes

  • Private revenge vs public justice: the judge who can't get justice.
  • Christian ethics vs Senecan revenge: ‘Vengeance is mine, saith the Lord’ (Romans 12:19) against Seneca's ‘the safe way to crime is through more crime’.
  • Madness and grief: Hieronimo and Isabella; parental loss.
  • Court corruption and Machiavellian politics (Lorenzo).
  • Language failing: letters, sundry languages (a Babel), the bitten-out tongue.
  • Metatheatre: a play-within-a-play; Andrea and Revenge as audience; theatre as a weapon.
  • Providence or fate: Revenge ‘sleeps’ in Act 3, but everything still ends as he promised.

The Turk

  • The fatal play-within-a-play is set at the Ottoman court of Suleiman (Soliman), on Rhodes. The Turk becomes the image of tyranny, lust and cruelty, and the stage where Spanish nobles die.
  • Kyd probably later wrote a full play, Soliman and Perseda (c. 1590).

Revenge-tragedy checklist (later in Hamlet)

  • A ghost · a revenger with a just cause but no legal remedy · delay and doubt · madness (real or feigned) · a Machiavel villain · a play-within-a-play or masque · gore · the revenger dies too.
  • Kyd may have written the lost ‘Ur-Hamlet’.

Britannica's take (her handout)

  • An early revenge tragedy (Britannica dates it c. 1591): a father seeks justice for his son but, in an unjust world, can get it only by taking the law into his own hands.
  • Kyd puts Senecan conventions (a ghost impatient for revenge) into a Christian setting: a genuine clash of values, so Hieronimo's success is at once triumphant and horrifying.
  • Britannica calls Kyd Marlowe's friend and says the play has the same effect as Marlowe's: a dilemma the audience can neither resolve nor ignore.

Ammo: lines to quote

Here sit we down to see the mystery, / And serve for Chorus in this tragedy.
Revenge, 1.1 · Frame and metatheatre.
What outcries pluck me from my naked bed
Hieronimo, 2.5 · Discovery of Horatio's body.
O eyes, no eyes, but fountains fraught with tears
Hieronimo, 3.2 · Patterned, rhetorical grief (Senecan style).
Vindicta mihi!
Hieronimo, 3.13 · ‘Vengeance is mine’: Christian patience vs revenge.
Per scelus semper tutum est sceleribus iter.
Hieronimo quoting Seneca, 3.13 · ‘The safe way to crime is through more crime.’
Why then I'll fit you.
Hieronimo, 4.1 · Double meaning: he'll supply the play, and give them what they deserve.
What they’ll askFavourite essay topics: justice vs revenge; metatheatre; is Hieronimo a hero or a villain?; the Machiavel; women's agency (Bel-imperia, Isabella).
W5Marlowe, Tamburlaine the Great, Part I

A Scythian shepherd talks and fights his way to world empire, cages the Ottoman sultan, slaughters virgins, marries the Egyptian princess, and is never punished. The first great overreacher, in thundering blank verse. (Fun fact: the real Timur beat the real Bayezid I near Ankara in 1402.)

Basics

  • Marlowe, c. 1587, for the Admiral's Men, with Edward Alleyn as Tamburlaine; printed 1590. Part II followed because Part I was a hit.
  • Historical model: Timur (Temür, 1336–1405), who defeated and captured the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I at the Battle of Ankara (1402).
  • The Prologue rejects rhyming clown-comedy and promises high astounding terms: blank verse, epic scale, spectacle.

Who's who

  • Tamburlaine: Scythian shepherd turned conqueror.
  • Zenocrate: daughter of the Soldan of Egypt; captured, falls in love with him.
  • Theridamas: Persian general won over by Tamburlaine's speech. Techelles, Usumcasane: his followers.
  • Mycetes: weak, silly King of Persia. Cosroe: his brother, who uses Tamburlaine and is betrayed.
  • Bajazeth: Emperor of the Turks (the Ottoman sultan). Zabina: his empress.
  • Soldan of Egypt; King of Arabia (Zenocrate's betrothed); Governor of Damascus; Virgins of Damascus; Agydas.

Plot

  • Act 1: Mycetes sends Theridamas against Tamburlaine, who has captured Zenocrate. Tamburlaine wins Theridamas over with words, not swords.
  • Act 2: Cosroe allies with him to depose Mycetes, then Tamburlaine turns on Cosroe (‘ride in triumph through Persepolis’; the ‘aspiring minds’ speech) and becomes King of Persia.
  • Act 3: Bajazeth, besieging Constantinople, insults him. They fight; Zenocrate and Zabina trade insults; Bajazeth is defeated.
  • Act 4: Bajazeth is kept in a cage and used as Tamburlaine's footstool. Siege of Damascus, Zenocrate's father's city: white tents on day one (mercy), red on day two (fighting men die), black on day three (everyone dies).
  • Act 5: the Virgins of Damascus beg for mercy; he has them killed and hung on the walls. Bajazeth and Zabina dash their brains out against the cage. Zenocrate laments. Tamburlaine defeats the Soldan and Arabia (Arabia dies), spares the Soldan for Zenocrate, and crowns her Queen of Persia. Triumph and marriage, no fall.

Themes

  • The overreacher (Harry Levin's term): limitless aspiration, rising above your birth.
  • Fortune's wheel: tragedy normally shows it turning down; Tamburlaine claims to turn it himself.
  • The power of rhetoric: persuasion as conquest.
  • *Machiavellian virtù, cruelty and spectacle; Tamburlaine as the ‘scourge of God’*.
  • The earthly crown as the highest good: shocking (a heretical idea) and unpunished in Part I.
  • Social mobility: a shepherd breaking the Great Chain of Being.

Turks and the East

  • Bajazeth is the Ottoman sultan humiliated on stage. For an audience that feared Ottoman power, the caged sultan is a fantasy of revenge.
  • But it's complicated: Tamburlaine is also Eastern, England was trading with the Ottomans, and ‘the Turk’ works as a mirror for pride and tyranny that the West shares. Bajazeth and Zabina's deaths even get some pathos.

Britannica's take (her handout)

  • Marlowe's heroes are men of towering ambition speaking blank verse of unprecedented (sometimes monotonous) elevation; their ‘high astounding terms’ challenge the orthodox values of the societies they disrupt.
  • In Tamburlaine (two parts, published 1590) traditional political orders are overwhelmed by a conqueror who ignores the boasted legitimacy of weak kings (Mycetes, Bajazeth).
  • The point of all his plays: society's moral and religious sanctions are useless against pragmatic, amoral will. They speak to an age being changed by new politics, commerce and science.
  • His verse turns stage presence into power and pulls our sympathy toward the villain-hero: dilemmas that can be neither resolved nor ignored, the divided consciousness of the time.

Ammo: lines to quote

From jigging veins of rhyming mother-wits, / And such conceits as clownage keeps in pay, / We'll lead you to the stately tent of war
Prologue · New kind of drama: blank verse, war, grandeur.
Threat'ning the world with high astounding terms
Prologue · Power of language.
I hold the Fates bound fast in iron chains, / And with my hand turn Fortune's wheel about
Tamburlaine, 1.2 · Defying Fortune.
Is it not passing brave to be a king, / And ride in triumph through Persepolis?
Tamburlaine, 2.5 · Earthly glory as desire.
Nature, that framed us of four elements / Warring within our breasts for regiment, / Doth teach us all to have aspiring minds
Tamburlaine, 2.7 · The overreacher's manifesto.
The sweet fruition of an earthly crown.
Tamburlaine, 2.7 · Bathos: infinite aspiration ends in a crown.
Ah, fair Zenocrate, divine Zenocrate
Tamburlaine, 5.1 · Beauty, and the limits of words.
What they’ll askTypical questions: ‘Hero or monster?’, ‘Marlowe's overreacher’, ‘The representation of the Turk in Tamburlaine’, ‘Rhetoric and power’.
W7Marlowe, Doctor Faustus

A brilliant scholar sells his soul for 24 years of power and spends it on cheap tricks, then has one hour to watch his damnation arrive. Renaissance ambition inside a medieval morality play. Taught Nov 4, a week before the exam. Read it before class.

Basics

  • Marlowe, c. 1588–92 (syllabus: 1592). Two texts: the A-text (1604) and the longer B-text (1616), which has more comedy and is more orthodox.
  • Source: the English Faust Book (1592), from the German Faustbuch (1587).
  • A hybrid: Renaissance tragedy plus a medieval morality play (Good and Evil Angels, the Seven Deadly Sins, the Old Man).

Who's who

  • Faustus: Wittenberg doctor of divinity. Wagner: his servant. Good Angel / Evil Angel.
  • Valdes and Cornelius: magicians who tempt him. Mephistopheles (Mephastophilis), Lucifer, Beelzebub.
  • The Seven Deadly Sins; Robin, Rafe (Dick in the B-text): comic servants who parody conjuring.
  • The Pope; Emperor Charles V; a Knight; the Horse-courser; the Duke and Duchess of Vanholt; the Old Man; Helen of Troy (a spirit); the Scholars.

Plot

  • Prologue: a low-born man rises through learning, ‘swoll'n with cunning’ like Icarus, and the heavens melt his wax wings.
  • 1.1: Faustus rejects logic, medicine, law and divinity. He reads Romans 6:23 (‘the reward of sin is death’) and 1 John 1:8 (‘if we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves’), but cuts off each verse before its promise of grace, concludes we must sin and die (‘Che sarà, sarà’), and turns to necromancy.
  • 1.3: he conjures Mephistopheles, who says he came because Faustus rejected God, not because of the spell: ‘Why, this is hell, nor am I out of it’. Faustus offers his soul for 24 years of service.
  • 2.1: he signs in blood, which congeals; ‘Consummatum est’ (Christ's last words, blasphemously); ‘Homo, fuge’ (‘Man, fly!’) appears on his arm. Devils distract him with a show. He asks for a wife (gets a devil), asks who made the world (refused), wants to repent, and Lucifer distracts him with the Seven Deadly Sins.
  • Act 3: invisible in Rome, he plays tricks on the Pope (snatches food, boxes his ears). Anti-Catholic farce.
  • Act 4: for Emperor Charles V he conjures Alexander the Great; puts horns on a mocking knight; cheats a horse-courser (the horse turns into hay); brings grapes in winter for the Duchess of Vanholt. Meanwhile the servants copy his conjuring.
  • 5.1: scholars ask to see Helen. The Old Man urges repentance; Faustus despairs, Mephistopheles threatens him, and he asks for Helen as his lover: ‘Was this the face…’.
  • 5.2: the final hour. The clock strikes eleven, half past, midnight. He begs time to stop, sees Christ's blood in the sky, wishes to dissolve into mist or water drops. Devils drag him off: ‘I'll burn my books!’
  • Epilogue: ‘Cut is the branch…’, a warning not to practise more than heaven permits.

Themes

  • Knowledge and power: the overreacher again, but turned inward and toward God.
  • Renaissance individualism vs the medieval Christian order.
  • Damnation and predestination: Calvinist debate. Is Faustus a reprobate who can't repent, or a free man who won't? His real sin may be despair.
  • Trivialisation of power: he dreams of empire (1.1, 1.3) and ends up doing magic tricks for dukes.
  • Hell as a state of mind (Mephistopheles' lines).
  • Anti-Catholicism (the Pope scenes) and comedy as parody (servants copying the master).

Tragic shape

  • Rise → fall; hamartia (pride, despair); late anagnorisis in the last soliloquy; catharsis through pity and fear in the final hour.

Britannica's take (her handout)

  • Doctor Faustus (Britannica: c. 1593, published 1604) depicts the overthrow of a man whose learning shows scant regard for God.
  • The same Marlowe pattern as Tamburlaine: limitless will against the moral order. This time the order wins, but the verse still makes us side with Faustus.
  • From the Renaissance handout: Calvinism made tragic heroes ‘victims of divine purposes that are terrifying yet inscrutable’. Use it in the fate-or-choice essay.
  • Other Marlowe plays to name: Edward II (a weak king destroyed) and The Jew of Malta (its prologue is spoken by Machiavelli).

Ammo: lines to quote

His waxen wings did mount above his reach, / And melting heavens conspired his overthrow.
Prologue · Icarus image: overreaching.
A sound magician is a mighty god.
Faustus, 1.1 · Magic as a shortcut to godhood.
Why, this is hell, nor am I out of it.
Mephistopheles, 1.3 · Hell as inner state, loss of God.
Consummatum est.
Faustus, 2.1 · Blasphemous echo of Christ on the cross.
Was this the face that launched a thousand ships / And burnt the topless towers of Ilium? / Sweet Helen, make me immortal with a kiss.
Faustus, 5.1 · Beauty as a false immortality; demonic union.
Ah, Faustus, / Now hast thou but one bare hour to live, / And then thou must be damned perpetually.
Faustus, 5.2 · Time running out.
See, see where Christ's blood streams in the firmament!
Faustus, 5.2 · Grace visible but out of reach.
Cut is the branch that might have grown full straight, / And burnèd is Apollo's laurel bough
Epilogue · Wasted genius; moral of the play.
What they’ll askClassic essays: ‘Faustus and Tamburlaine as overreachers’; ‘Is Faustus damned by fate or by choice?’; ‘Morality-play elements in Doctor Faustus’; ‘The comic scenes: padding or meaning?’
EXTRAConnections: revenger, overreacher, the Turk

Long-answer questions in this course like comparison. Here's the whole first half on one screen.

Everything at once

Spanish TragedyTamburlaine IDoctor FaustusSonnets
DriveJustice, revengeThe earthly crownUnlimited knowledge and powerKeep the beloved alive
What blocks itA corrupt court; the lawNothing (unpunished)God; his own despairTime
EndingBloodbath, revenge achievedTriumph and marriageDamnationThe poem outlives Time
FormSenecan revenge tragedy, metatheatreHeroic drama, spectacleTragedy + morality playEnglish sonnet
LanguagePatterned, rhetorical lamentThe ‘mighty line’, persuasionSoaring verse, Latin tags, final soliloquyCompressed conceits
The Turk / East‘Soliman and Perseda’ play-within-a-playBajazeth caged as footstoolFaustus dreams of world empire—

Key terms

  • Overreacher: Harry Levin, The Overreacher: A Study of Christopher Marlowe (1952). The hero whose desire has no limit (Tamburlaine, Faustus).
  • Revenge tragedy: Senecan model; Kyd's checklist (ghost, delay, madness, Machiavel, play-within-play, bloody end).
  • Machiavel: the stage villain who delights in plotting (Lorenzo).
  • Morality play: medieval allegorical drama about the soul's struggle (Everyman); angels, vices, sins.
  • Metatheatre: a play aware of being theatre (Revenge and Andrea watching; ‘Soliman and Perseda’; Faustus staging spirits).
  • Turning Turk: converting to Islam, or betraying one's own side. The Turk as a figure of tyranny, lust and cruelty, and of wealth and power.
What they’ll askIf a question says ‘with reference to two plays’, this table is your skeleton. Pick one row (drive, ending, form) and build the comparison around it.

Shakespeare // Flashcards

Cover the answer, say it out loud, then check.

  1. Rhyme scheme of a Shakespearean sonnet
    ABAB CDCD EFEF GG: three quatrains and a couplet, iambic pentameter.
  2. Petrarchan vs Shakespearean sonnet
    Petrarchan: octave + sestet (ABBAABBA CDECDE). Shakespearean: 3 quatrains + couplet.
  3. Volta
    The ‘turn’ in a sonnet's argument. In 18 it comes at line 9: ‘But thy eternal summer shall not fade’.
  4. Fair Youth vs Dark Lady sonnets
    1–126 Fair Youth (1–17: procreation); 127–152 Dark Lady.
  5. Sonnet 18: main idea
    The beloved is better than summer; the poem will make his beauty eternal.
  6. Sonnet 60: main idea
    Time destroys everything (waves, scythe), but the poem will stand.
  7. Sonnet 130: main idea
    Anti-Petrarchan: mocks fancy comparisons; real love needs no ‘false compare’.
  8. Blazon
    A poem listing a woman's beauties part by part with comparisons. Sonnet 130 parodies it.
  9. When was the sonnet sequence published?
    1609, by Thomas Thorpe, dedicated to ‘Mr. W. H.’
  10. The Theatre (1576)
    First purpose-built London playhouse, by James Burbage.
  11. The Rose
    Philip Henslowe's playhouse (1587) on Bankside; home of the Admiral's Men and Marlowe's plays.
  12. Edward Alleyn
    Star actor of the Admiral's Men; played Tamburlaine and Faustus.
  13. University Wits
    Marlowe, Greene, Peele, Lyly, Nashe, Lodge: university men writing for the popular stage.
  14. Blank verse
    Unrhymed iambic pentameter. Marlowe's ‘mighty line’ (Jonson's phrase).
  15. Machiavel
    Stage villain who plots with cunning and enjoys it. Lorenzo in The Spanish Tragedy.
  16. Senecan tragedy features
    Five acts, ghosts, revenge, horror, long rhetorical speeches, Latin tags.
  17. Master of the Revels
    Official who licensed and censored plays.
  18. Why were playhouses outside the City?
    To escape the City authorities, who were hostile (Puritanism, plague, disorder).
  19. Levant Company
    English trading company with the Ottoman Empire (Turkey Company 1581; Levant Company 1592).
  20. Who is the frame chorus in The Spanish Tragedy?
    The Ghost of Andrea and Revenge.
  21. How is Horatio killed?
    Hanged in the arbour and stabbed by Lorenzo, Balthazar and their men.
  22. Bel-imperia's letter
    Written in blood; names Lorenzo and Balthazar as Horatio's murderers.
  23. Pedringano's box
    He thinks a boy's box holds his pardon, so he jokes on the gallows. It's empty.
  24. ‘Vindicta mihi’
    ‘Vengeance is mine’ (Romans 12:19). Hieronimo weighs God's justice against his own revenge.
  25. The play-within-the-play in Kyd
    ‘Soliman and Perseda’, set at the Turkish court, performed in sundry languages; the deaths are real.
  26. How does Hieronimo end?
    Bites out his tongue, stabs the Duke of Castile, then kills himself with a penknife.
  27. Who is Lorenzo?
    Bel-imperia's brother; the Machiavel who plots Horatio's murder.
  28. Ur-Hamlet
    A lost earlier Hamlet play, possibly by Kyd.
  29. Historical Tamburlaine
    Timur (Temür), who defeated Bayezid I at the Battle of Ankara, 1402.
  30. Who plays Tamburlaine's footstool?
    Bajazeth, the Turkish emperor, kept in a cage.
  31. White, red, black tents
    Damascus siege: day 1 mercy; day 2 death to fighting men; day 3 death to all.
  32. How do Bajazeth and Zabina die?
    They dash their brains out against the cage.
  33. Who is Zenocrate?
    Daughter of the Soldan of Egypt; Tamburlaine's captive and then his queen.
  34. Theridamas
    Persian general won over by Tamburlaine's eloquence.
  35. ‘Overreacher’ comes from…
    Harry Levin, The Overreacher (1952), about Marlowe's heroes.
  36. How does Tamburlaine I end?
    In triumph: truce with the Soldan, Zenocrate crowned Queen of Persia. No fall.
  37. Doctor Faustus: A-text vs B-text
    A-text 1604 (shorter); B-text 1616 (longer, more comedy, more orthodox).
  38. How does Faustus misread the Bible?
    He quotes Romans 6:23 and 1 John 1:8 but stops before the promise of grace, so concludes damnation is inevitable.
  39. How long is Faustus' contract?
    24 years.
  40. ‘Homo, fuge’
    ‘Man, fly!’: appears on Faustus' arm after he signs in blood.
  41. ‘Consummatum est’
    ‘It is finished’: Christ's last words, said by Faustus after signing. Blasphemy.
  42. ‘Why, this is hell, nor am I out of it’
    Mephistopheles (1.3): hell is the loss of God, a state, not just a place.
  43. Morality-play elements in Faustus
    Good and Evil Angels, Seven Deadly Sins, the Old Man, the fight for a soul.
  44. Who does Faustus conjure for Charles V?
    Alexander the Great (and his paramour).
  45. Source of Doctor Faustus
    The English Faust Book (1592), from the German Faustbuch (1587).
  46. Faustus' last line
    ‘I'll burn my books! Ah, Mephistopheles!’
  47. Prologue image in Faustus
    Icarus: waxen wings melting.
  48. How did Marlowe die?
    Stabbed in Deptford in 1593 by Ingram Frizer.
  49. Renaissance literally means…
    Rebirth: an awakening after the ‘Dark Ages’.
  50. Humanism (her handout)
    The belief, drawn from Greek and Roman thought, that humans can reach earthly perfection; optimistic and individual-centred.
  51. English Renaissance: dates
    Her intro handout: 1500–1660. The Britannica article: 1550–1660.
  52. Elizabethan vs Jacobean
    Elizabethan: Elizabeth I, 1558–1603. Jacobean: James I, 1603–1625.
  53. Why did More write Utopia in Latin?
    English was looked down on as unfit for serious learning.
  54. Gutenberg's key innovation
    Fast movable type (c. 1440/1450): cheap, quick printing.
  55. Three effects of printing (her handout)
    More literacy, the spread of the Reformation (Luther's 95 Theses), the democratisation of reading.
  56. How did printing change reading?
    From reading aloud in groups to silent, individual reading.
  57. Caxton
    Brought printing to England in 1476; first English printed book: The Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye (Bruges, 1473–74).
  58. Britannica's ‘doubleness’
    New possibilities and new doubts at the same time: the source of the period's intensity.
  59. Calvinism and Jacobean tragedy
    Heroes are victims of terrifying, inscrutable divine purposes, not masters of their fate.
  60. Castiglione's The Courtier
    Translated by Hoby (1561): wit, sprezzatura, Neoplatonic love of beauty.
  61. Sprezzatura
    Accomplishment that looks effortless (Castiglione).
  62. The Prince in England
    Written 1513, no English translation until 1640; attacked in public, read in private.
  63. Patronage
    Rich nobles funding artists; works dedicated to patrons, sometimes to several at once.
  64. Why did the English Renaissance end? (her handout)
    Cynicism and decadence, Puritanism, and Elizabeth's lack of an heir.
  65. The Red Lion
    One of the first commercial playhouses, built in 1567 outside London.
  66. Why did the Puritans attack the theatre?
    Cross-dressing and play-acting would spread sexual corruption; plus crowds, idleness, pubs and brothels.
  67. Gorboduc (1561)
    Sackville and Norton's Senecan tragedy: the earliest known English play in blank verse.
  68. The Vice
    The tricky villain of the morality play; lives on in Richard III.
  69. Court masque
    Lavish song-and-dance shows for James I and Charles I (Jonson and Inigo Jones).
  70. Britannica on the University Wits
    Social pretensions, but middle-class, patriotic, romantic drama (Peele, Greene, Lyly).
  71. Britannica on Marlowe's plays
    Society's moral and religious sanctions are useless against pragmatic, amoral will.
  72. Britannica on The Spanish Tragedy
    Senecan revenge in a Christian setting: Hieronimo's success is both triumphant and horrifying.
  73. New English words 1500–1650
    About 10,000–12,000, roughly half still in use.
  74. The Great Vowel Shift
    15th–17th c.: long vowels raised and moved forward; separates Middle from Modern English.
  75. Five dialect areas before print
    Northern, West Midlands, East Midlands (incl. London), Southern, Kentish.
  76. -eth vs -s
    Southern goeth vs northern goes; the northern -s won.
  77. Verbification
    Nouns used as verbs: ‘he pageants us’, ‘uncle me no uncle’, ‘it out-herods Herod’.
  78. Shakespeare's vocabulary and coinages
    About 34,000 words; about 2,000 neologisms (many just first recorded in his works).
  79. Five phrases from Shakespeare
    One fell swoop, brave new world, star-crossed lovers, it's Greek to me, cruel only to be kind.
  80. Turkish loanwords from the period
    Coffee, yoghurt, caviar, horde, chess, kiosk, tulip, turban.
  81. Shakespeare: birth and death
    Baptised 26 April 1564, Stratford-upon-Avon; died 23 April 1616.
  82. Shakespeare's company
    The Lord Chamberlain's Men (from c. 1594), later the King's Men.
  83. How many plays did Shakespeare write?
    37, c. 1590–1613.
  84. Shakespeare's last plays
    Tragicomedies: Cymbeline, The Winter's Tale, The Tempest, ending in reconciliation.
  85. Astrophel and Stella
    Sidney; written 1582, published 1591; started the sonnet-sequence craze.
  86. Spenser's Amoretti (1595)
    A sonnet sequence unusual for celebrating love fulfilled in marriage.
  87. Britannica on Shakespeare's sonnets
    Conventions upside down: a dark, treacherous lady and a male beloved.
  88. Negative capability
    Keats' phrase for Shakespeare's power to hold every attitude without settling on one.
  89. The Faerie Queene
    Spenser (1590–96): Protestant national epic mixing romance, epic and pastoral; Gloriana = Elizabeth.

Shakespeare // Quiz

  1. Which rhyme scheme is a Shakespearean sonnet?
    1. ABBAABBA CDECDE
    2. ABAB CDCD EFEF GG
    3. AABB CCDD EEFF GG
    4. ABAB BCBC CDCD EE
    Answer: B. Three quatrains and a couplet. The last option is Spenserian.
  2. Sonnet 130 is best described as…
    1. Petrarchan praise
    2. anti-Petrarchan parody
    3. a procreation sonnet
    4. a religious sonnet
    Answer: B. It denies every conventional comparison.
  3. Who serves as chorus in The Spanish Tragedy?
    1. The King of Spain
    2. Hieronimo
    3. The Ghost of Andrea and Revenge
    4. Bel-imperia
    Answer: C. They watch the whole action.
  4. Where is Horatio murdered?
    1. In the palace
    2. On the battlefield
    3. In the arbour
    4. In prison
    Answer: C. Isabella later cuts the arbour down.
  5. What does Pedringano believe the boy's box contains?
    1. Poison
    2. Gold
    3. His pardon
    4. A letter from Bel-imperia
    Answer: C. It's empty: Lorenzo's trick.
  6. The play-within-the-play in Kyd is set…
    1. In ancient Rome
    2. At the Ottoman (Turkish) court
    3. In Portugal
    4. In hell
    Answer: B. ‘Soliman and Perseda’.
  7. Tamburlaine begins as a…
    1. prince of Persia
    2. Scythian shepherd
    3. Turkish general
    4. Egyptian merchant
    Answer: B. His low birth is the whole point.
  8. Who is used as Tamburlaine's footstool?
    1. Mycetes
    2. Cosroe
    3. Bajazeth
    4. The Soldan
    Answer: C. The Turkish emperor, in a cage.
  9. How does Tamburlaine Part I end?
    1. Tamburlaine dies of illness
    2. Tamburlaine is defeated
    3. Tamburlaine marries Zenocrate in triumph
    4. Zenocrate kills herself
    Answer: C. No fall in Part I.
  10. Who coined the term ‘overreacher’ for Marlowe's heroes?
    1. Ben Jonson
    2. Harry Levin
    3. T. S. Eliot
    4. Stephen Greenblatt
    Answer: B. The Overreacher (1952).
  11. How long does Faustus' pact last?
    1. 7 years
    2. 12 years
    3. 24 years
    4. 40 years
    Answer: C. Twenty-four years of service from Mephistopheles.
  12. ‘Why, this is hell, nor am I out of it’ is said by…
    1. Faustus
    2. Lucifer
    3. Mephistopheles
    4. The Evil Angel
    Answer: C. 1.3: hell as the loss of God.
  13. Which is a morality-play element in Doctor Faustus?
    1. The Chorus
    2. Good and Evil Angels
    3. Helen of Troy
    4. The Horse-courser
    Answer: B. Plus the Seven Deadly Sins and the Old Man.
  14. Faustus misreads the Bible by…
    1. quoting it in Greek
    2. cutting off verses before the promise of grace
    3. denying God exists
    4. reading the Koran instead
    Answer: B. Romans 6:23 and 1 John 1:8 are both cut short.
  15. Which actor made Tamburlaine and Faustus famous?
    1. Richard Burbage
    2. Will Kemp
    3. Edward Alleyn
    4. Ben Jonson
    Answer: C. Alleyn, of the Admiral's Men.
  16. The Battle of Ankara (1402) matters because…
    1. Elizabeth I watched it
    2. Timur defeated Bayezid I there
    3. Marlowe was born there
    4. Kyd set a play there
    Answer: B. The historical basis of Tamburlaine vs Bajazeth.
  17. Which Latin phrase does Faustus say after signing?
    1. Vindicta mihi
    2. Consummatum est
    3. Carpe diem
    4. Memento mori
    Answer: B. Christ's last words: blasphemy. ‘Vindicta mihi’ is Hieronimo's.
  18. ‘Renaissance’ literally means…
    1. reform
    2. rebirth
    3. revolution
    4. return
    Answer: B. An awakening after the ‘Dark Ages’.
  19. Jacobean literature belongs to the reign of…
    1. Elizabeth I
    2. James I
    3. Charles I
    4. Henry VIII
    Answer: B. 1603–1625.
  20. Which is NOT an effect of printing in her handout?
    1. Rising literacy
    2. The spread of Luther's ideas
    3. Silent individual reading
    4. The end of patronage
    Answer: D. Writers still chased patrons.
  21. The earliest known English play in blank verse is…
    1. Tamburlaine
    2. Gorboduc
    3. The Spanish Tragedy
    4. Cambises
    Answer: B. Sackville and Norton, 1561.
  22. Why did the Puritans object to plays?
    1. They were in Latin
    2. Cross-dressing and play-acting would corrupt morals
    3. They praised the Pope
    4. They were too expensive
    Answer: B. Plus crowds, idleness, pubs and brothels.
  23. The Great Vowel Shift changed mainly…
    1. short vowels
    2. long vowels
    3. consonants
    4. spelling only
    Answer: B. Long vowels moved higher and further forward.
  24. Who brought printing to England in 1476?
    1. Gutenberg
    2. Caxton
    3. Tyndale
    4. Tottel
    Answer: B. His best sellers included Chaucer and Malory.
  25. ‘Uncle me no uncle’ is an example of…
    1. a blazon
    2. verbification
    3. a volta
    4. an aside
    Answer: B. A noun used as a verb.
  26. Britannica says Marlowe's plays show that…
    1. virtue always wins
    2. moral and religious sanctions are useless against amoral will
    3. kings are sacred
    4. comedy should instruct
    Answer: B. Hence our uneasy sympathy for his villain-heroes.
  27. Which sonnet sequence started the 1590s craze?
    1. Amoretti
    2. Delia
    3. Astrophel and Stella
    4. Idea's Mirror
    Answer: C. Sidney, published 1591.
  28. According to Britannica, Calvinism made Jacobean tragic heroes…
    1. masters of their fate
    2. victims of inscrutable divine purposes
    3. comic figures
    4. Catholic martyrs
    Answer: B. Useful for the Faustus fate-or-choice question.

Shakespeare // Write

Long essay template

  1. Intro (3–4 sentences): context → the key term in the question → your thesis (an argument, not a summary).
  2. Three body paragraphs: point → evidence (short quote or precise scene) → analysis → link back to the question.
  3. Comparing two texts? Compare inside each paragraph.
  4. Conclusion: answer the question, then one wider point.
  5. 40 minutes: 5 plan, 30 write, 5 proofread.

Short-answer template

  1. Define or identify in one sentence.
  2. One specific example from a text.
  3. Why it matters.
  4. Stop at 3–5 sentences.

Short answers (model answers)

  1. What is a ‘Machiavel’? Give an example.
    A stage villain modelled on the English (mis)reading of Machiavelli: a cunning, amoral plotter who enjoys manipulation. Lorenzo in The Spanish Tragedy is one: he arranges Horatio's murder, then removes his accomplices (Serberine, Pedringano) to hide his guilt.
  2. Explain the significance of the ‘Vindicta mihi’ soliloquy.
    In 3.13 Hieronimo quotes Romans 12:19 (‘Vengeance is mine’), the Christian command to leave revenge to God, then switches to Seneca's advice that crime is safest when followed by more crime. The speech dramatises the conflict between Christian patience and private revenge and marks his decision to act in secret.
  3. What is the function of the Prologue in Tamburlaine Part I?
    It rejects rhymed, clownish popular drama (‘jigging veins of rhyming mother-wits’) and promises war and ‘high astounding terms’. It announces Marlowe's new blank-verse heroic drama, and tells the audience to judge Tamburlaine for themselves.
  4. Why is Bajazeth important?
    Bajazeth, the Turkish emperor, is defeated, caged and used as Tamburlaine's footstool, then kills himself with Zabina. He embodies Western fears and fantasies about Ottoman power, but his and Zabina's suffering also gets pathos. Historically, Timur defeated Bayezid I at Ankara in 1402.
  5. Explain ‘Why, this is hell, nor am I out of it’.
    Mephistopheles tells Faustus that hell is not just a place but the condition of being deprived of God. Having seen heaven, he suffers its loss everywhere. It foreshadows Faustus' own fate and shows the devils are honest about damnation while Faustus refuses to listen.
  6. What is the volta in Sonnet 18?
    At line 9 (‘But thy eternal summer shall not fade’) the poem turns from listing summer's faults to the claim that the beloved's beauty is eternal, because it is preserved in the poet's ‘eternal lines’. The couplet completes the turn: the poem gives life to the youth.
  7. Why was the printing press important for the Renaissance?
    Gutenberg's movable type made books quick and cheap to copy. Literacy rose, Luther's 95 Theses and the Reformation spread, and literature stopped being a privilege of the few. Reading changed from reading aloud to groups to silent, individual interpretation. In England Caxton began printing in 1476, which also helped fix spelling.
  8. Explain Britannica's idea of the ‘doubleness’ of the period.
    The Elizabethan and Jacobean age looks radiant and confident, yet it was a time of traumatic strain: prices and population soared, the new science unsettled the cosmos, the religious compromise was fragile and Calvinism told people they were helpless. New possibilities and new doubts arrived together, and that tension gives the literature its intensity.
  9. Why did the Puritans attack the theatre?
    They saw it as immoral: boys dressed as women and actors pretended to be what they were not, which supposedly encouraged sexual corruption. Locals also complained about crowds, noise, idleness and the pubs and brothels around the playhouses. The Puritans finally closed the theatres in 1642.
  10. What is the Great Vowel Shift?
    A major change in English pronunciation in the 15th–17th centuries: long vowels were raised and moved further forward in the mouth, while short vowels stayed largely the same. It separates Middle from Modern English, so Chaucer would sound almost foreign today while Shakespeare would only sound accented.

Essay questions with battle plans

  1. Compare Tamburlaine and Faustus as ‘overreachers’.
    1. Thesis: both refuse the limits set by birth and God, but Tamburlaine's desire points outward (crowns, conquest) and is rewarded, while Faustus' points upward (knowledge, godhood) and is damned.
    2. Context: Renaissance humanism and social mobility vs the Great Chain of Being; Calvinist theology. Levin's term.
    3. Tamburlaine: ‘aspiring minds’ speech; Fortune's wheel in his hand; rhetoric as conquest; no punishment in Part I.
    4. Faustus: ‘a sound magician is a mighty god’; 24-year pact; trivial use of power; final hour; the Icarus prologue.
    5. Form: heroic spectacle vs morality-play structure (Angels, Sins).
    6. Conclusion: Marlowe tests the limits of human ambition from two sides; the ‘mighty line’ makes both seductive.
  2. Private revenge and public justice in The Spanish Tragedy.
    1. Thesis: Kyd shows a justice system so corrupt that a judge becomes a murderer. Revenge is condemned by Christianity but presented as the only option.
    2. Context: Senecan revenge; English law and the Crown's monopoly on justice; Romans 12:19.
    3. Hieronimo the judge: Lorenzo blocks access to the King; petitioners scene; ‘Vindicta mihi’.
    4. Revenge by theatre: ‘Soliman and Perseda’; real deaths; sundry languages.
    5. Frame: Revenge and Andrea show that a cosmic revenge plot runs above human justice.
    6. Conclusion: ambiguity. Hieronimo achieves justice and becomes a mass murderer. The model for Hamlet.
  3. How are Turks represented in the plays you have studied?
    1. Thesis: the Turk is a figure of tyranny and pride, and a mirror for European desires for power, shaped by fear of and trade with the Ottoman Empire.
    2. Context: Lepanto 1571, Levant Company, Elizabeth and Murad III, ‘turning Turk’.
    3. Tamburlaine: Bajazeth's arrogance, cage, footstool, suicide; the historical Battle of Ankara; pathos in Zabina.
    4. Spanish Tragedy: ‘Soliman and Perseda’ as the stage of killing; the Turkish court as tyranny and lust.
    5. Complication: Tamburlaine is Eastern too; Western courts (Spain) are just as corrupt.
    6. Conclusion: stereotypes that also reflect English anxieties and ambitions.
  4. Is Faustus damned by fate or by choice?
    1. Thesis: the play keeps both readings open. Calvinist predestination vs free will. But it dramatises despair as Faustus' decisive sin.
    2. Fate: misreading of scripture; ‘Che sarà, sarà’; Mephistopheles' threats; the Icarus prologue.
    3. Choice: Good Angel and Old Man keep offering repentance; he repeatedly chooses distraction (Sins, Helen).
    4. Final hour: ‘Christ's blood streams in the firmament’, grace visible but unreachable to a despairing mind.
    5. Conclusion: the tragedy is that he believes he can't repent.
  5. Time and poetic immortality in Sonnets 18 and 60 (with 130 as contrast).
    1. Thesis: 18 and 60 set poetry against Time's destruction; 130 questions the poetic conventions that make such praise possible.
    2. 18: summer's faults; volta at 9; ‘eternal lines’; the couplet's self-praise.
    3. 60: waves/minutes; Nativity to eclipse; Time's scythe; ‘my verse shall stand’.
    4. 130: blazon parodied; ‘false compare’; truth over hyperbole.
    5. Form: quatrain development and couplet resolution.
    6. Conclusion: confidence in art's power, and suspicion of art's lies (contrast Faustus' Helen).
  6. Metatheatre in The Spanish Tragedy and Doctor Faustus.
    1. Thesis: both plays use theatre within theatre to show power: Hieronimo kills through a play, Faustus' magic is a series of shows.
    2. Kyd: Revenge and Andrea as audience; ‘Soliman and Perseda’; ‘Why then I'll fit you’.
    3. Marlowe: devils' dances, the Sins pageant, Alexander, Helen. Illusions that distract from salvation.
    4. Meaning: theatre as both truth-telling and deception; Elizabethan anti-theatrical worries (Gosson).
    5. Conclusion: the Renaissance stage questions its own power.
  7. What were the main characteristics of the English Renaissance?
    1. Definition: ‘rebirth’; a break with feudalism after the Dark Ages and the Black Death; England 1500/1550–1660.
    2. Humanism: classical learning, human perfectibility, optimism; Erasmian schooling; Italian models (Petrarch, Castiglione).
    3. Print: Gutenberg and Caxton; literacy, the Reformation, silent reading.
    4. Forms: poetry and drama; strict conventions; genre-mixing (The Faerie Queene).
    5. Court and patronage: wit, double meanings, dedications; the theatre as the focal point of the age.
    6. The doubleness (Britannica): social strain, new science, Calvinism, Machiavelli.
    7. The end: Puritanism, no heir, theatres closed 1642.
    8. Conclusion: a golden age built on tension, which is why its drama is so intense.
  8. How did the Renaissance change the English language, and what was Shakespeare's part?
    1. Before: English despised as unfit for learning (More's Latin Utopia).
    2. Words: 10–12k new words 1500–1650; deliberate Latin/Greek borrowing; Bacon's coinages; trade loanwords (Turkish coffee, kiosk, tulip).
    3. Sound: the Great Vowel Shift.
    4. Print: Caxton 1476; five dialects; chaotic spelling; -eth vs -s.
    5. Shakespeare: verbification (‘he pageants us’), 34,000-word vocabulary, about 2,000 coinages (with her caveat), everyday phrases.
    6. Conclusion: by 1600 English is confident enough for great literature, and Shakespeare is its showcase.

How to beat this exam

  • This course is practical. Expect to translate or analyse a short poem or children's text and justify your choices with named concepts. A translation without justification is half an answer.
  • Your readings are Moodle chapters and articles, so check the names there. The frameworks here are the standard ones that show up in almost every literary translation course: Dryden, Jakobson, Holmes, Lefevere, Nida, Venuti, Shavit, Klingberg, Oittinen.
  • Learning outcomes she'll grade: identify strategies and challenges, show sensitivity to tone, style and cultural context, and discuss how translation negotiates cultural borders.
  • Use the commentary template (Write tab): source-text analysis → global strategy → local choices → what's lost, what's gained, why.
  • Don't forget the take-home project (10%) due Nov 2. It's a separate grade, but it's also the best midterm practice you'll get.
