Translation // Intel

1Toolkit: the key concepts and debates

Every translation choice sits between two pulls: stay close to the source or make it work for the new reader. These are the names people gave to that tension. Learn them as pairs.

The big pairs

ConceptWhoSource-oriented sideTarget-oriented side
Two directionsSchleiermacher (1813)Move the reader toward the authorMove the author toward the reader
EquivalenceNida (1964)Formal equivalence: keep form and contentDynamic equivalence: same effect on the new reader
MethodNewmark (1981)Semantic translationCommunicative translation
StrategyVenuti (1995)Foreignization: keep the foreignness visibleDomestication: fluent, familiar, the translator becomes invisible

Other essentials

  • Dryden (1680): three kinds of translation: metaphrase (word by word), paraphrase (sense for sense, with latitude), imitation (free re-creation; words and sense can change).
  • Jakobson, “On Linguistic Aspects of Translation” (1959): intralingual (rewording), interlingual (translation proper), intersemiotic (into another sign system, e.g. novel → film). Poetry is “untranslatable”: only creative transposition is possible.
  • Skopos theory (Vermeer; Reiss & Vermeer): the purpose of the translation decides the method. Reiss' text types: informative, expressive (literature: focus on form and author), operative.
  • Vinay & Darbelnet procedures: direct (borrowing, calque, literal) and oblique (transposition, modulation, equivalence, adaptation).
  • Compensation: what you lose in one place (a pun, a rhyme) you recreate somewhere else.
  • Lefevere: translation is rewriting, shaped by ideology, poetics and patronage (who pays, who publishes).
  • Even-Zohar, polysystem theory: translated literature can be central (innovative, foreignizing) or peripheral (conservative, adapting) in the target culture. Key for children's literature.
  • Culture-specific items (Aixelá): conservation (keep, explain in a gloss) vs substitution (replace with something local, generalise, delete).
What they’ll askConcept questions usually ask you to define and illustrate one pair (domestication vs foreignization, formal vs dynamic). Always add a concrete example, ideally English↔Turkish.
3–4Translating poetry

Poetry is where meaning lives in sound, rhythm, rhyme and ambiguity at once, so something always dies. The question is what you choose to save, and whether you can make it live again in Turkish (or English).

What makes poetry hard

  • Form: meter, rhyme scheme, stanza shape, line length.
  • Sound: alliteration, assonance, onomatopoeia, rhythm.
  • Meaning density: ambiguity, connotation, puns, allusion, imagery.
  • Cultural load: religious or mythic references, forms that exist in one tradition only (the sonnet vs the gazel/koşma).
  • Jakobson's verdict: poetry is untranslatable; only creative transposition is possible.

Lefevere's seven strategies (Translating Poetry, 1975)

StrategyWhat it doesUsual cost
PhonemicImitates the source's soundsSense becomes awkward
LiteralWord for wordPoetic quality and syntax suffer
MetricalKeeps the original meterMeaning gets bent to fit
Poetry into proseTurns verse into proseLoses rhythm and form
RhymedKeeps rhymeForces word choice and meaning
Blank verseUnrhymed but metricalRhyme lost, more freedom
InterpretationVersion (same content, new form) or imitation (a new poem)Becomes the translator's poem

Holmes: four ways to handle verse form (1970)

  • Mimetic form: copy the original form (keep the sonnet, the rhyme scheme).
  • Analogical form: use the target culture's equivalent form (e.g. render a classical epic meter as English blank verse; a gazel as a sonnet?).
  • Organic (content-derivative) form: let the content shape a new form.
  • Extraneous (deviant) form: a form unrelated to the original.

Turkish ↔ English examples worth knowing

  • Shakespeare's sonnets in Turkish: Talât Sait Halman's versions stay closer to the source; Can Yücel labelled his free versions “Türkçe söyleyen” (“said in Turkish by”): domesticated imitations that sound like Turkish poems. A perfect Dryden/Lefevere/Venuti example.
  • Turkish poetry in English: Nazım Hikmet (Randy Blasing & Mutlu Konuk Blasing), Orhan Veli and Yunus Emre (Talât Halman). Problems: free verse vs syllabic folk meters, Sufi vocabulary (aşk, dost, gönül), vowel harmony and rhyme that English can't copy.
  • What dies first: rhyme and wordplay. Compensation is your weapon: recreate a sound effect or a pun in another line.
What they’ll askIf you get a poem: describe its form/sound/meaning features → choose a strategy (Lefevere/Holmes) and say why → name what you sacrificed and how you compensated. Mention domestication vs foreignization in one line.
5–7Translating children's literature

Children's books get changed more than any other translated literature: names are swapped, food is localised, scary or rude bits are cleaned up, and puns rewritten. Why? Because adults decide what's good for children, and children's literature sits at the edge of the literary system. Last unit taught Nov 2.

Why it's special

  • Dual audience: children read it, but adults choose, buy, approve and often read it aloud (parents, teachers, publishers = gatekeepers).
  • Ambivalent texts (Shavit): books like Alice in Wonderland work on two levels, for children and adults.
  • Illustrations: text and picture must still match after translation (Oittinen).
  • Read-aloud: rhythm and sound matter, because the text is performed.
  • Didactic pressure: translations are expected to teach and protect.

Key theorists

WhoMain idea
Zohar Shavit (1981, 1986)Because children's literature is peripheral in the polysystem, translators manipulate it freely, as long as they (1) make the text appropriate and useful for the child by society's educational norms and (2) adjust plot, characters and language to the child's assumed level of understanding.
Göte Klingberg (1986)Catalogues cultural context adaptation: added explanations, substituted local equivalents, deletion, modernisation, purification (cleaning up “unsuitable” content), abridgement. He's critical: too much adaptation betrays the source and the child's chance to meet another culture.
Riitta Oittinen (2000)Translating for Children: translation is dialogic (Bakhtin); translators translate for their image of the child; reading aloud and illustrations are part of the text. More open to adapting for the young reader.
Emer O'Sullivan (2005)The implied translator leaves traces in the text (explanations, omissions) that reveal who they think the reader is.
Eirlys Davies (2003)Strategies for culture-specific items, using Harry Potter: preservation, addition, omission, globalisation, localisation, transformation, creation.

Typical problems and options

  • Names: meaningful or funny names (Mrs. Tiggy-Winkle). Keep, translate the meaning, or invent a new funny name.
  • Wordplay and nonsense: Carroll's puns (‘tale/tail’). Usually needs creative substitution in the target language.
  • Parody: Carroll parodies poems every Victorian child knew. The translator must parody a poem Turkish children know, or the joke vanishes.
  • Rhyme and rhythm in nursery rhymes: keep the music even if the words change.
  • Food, festivals, money, school life: localise (Christmas pudding → something Turkish?) or preserve and let the child learn?
  • Purification: violence, death, rudeness, religion softened. Ask whether it protects the child or underestimates them.
What they’ll askEssay favourite: “Should translators adapt children's literature for the target culture?” Argue with Shavit (it happens and why), Klingberg (against too much), Oittinen (for the child reader), with one concrete example.

Translation // Flashcards

Cover the answer, say it out loud, then check.

  1. Dryden's three kinds of translation
    Metaphrase (word for word), paraphrase (sense for sense), imitation (free re-creation).
  2. Jakobson's three types of translation
    Intralingual (rewording), interlingual (translation proper), intersemiotic (into another sign system).
  3. Jakobson on poetry
    Poetry is untranslatable; only creative transposition is possible.
  4. Formal vs dynamic equivalence
    Nida: keep the source's form and content vs produce the same effect on the new reader.
  5. Semantic vs communicative translation
    Newmark: close to the source's meaning and form vs focused on the target reader's understanding.
  6. Domestication
    Venuti: fluent, familiar translation that hides foreignness and makes the translator invisible.
  7. Foreignization
    Venuti: translation that keeps the source's foreignness visible.
  8. Translator's invisibility
    Venuti (1995): fluent domesticated translations hide the translator's work.
  9. Schleiermacher's two methods
    Move the reader toward the author, or the author toward the reader.
  10. Skopos theory
    Vermeer, Reiss: the purpose of the translation determines the method.
  11. Reiss' text types
    Informative, expressive (literature), operative.
  12. Vinay & Darbelnet: direct procedures
    Borrowing, calque, literal translation.
  13. Vinay & Darbelnet: oblique procedures
    Transposition, modulation, equivalence, adaptation.
  14. Calque
    A loan translation: copying the structure of a foreign expression word by word.
  15. Modulation
    Changing the point of view (e.g. ‘it's not difficult’ → ‘it's easy’).
  16. Compensation
    Recreating a lost effect (pun, rhyme) somewhere else in the text.
  17. Lefevere: translation as…
    Rewriting, shaped by ideology, poetics and patronage.
  18. Polysystem theory
    Even-Zohar: translated literature can be central or peripheral in the target literary system.
  19. Lefevere's seven poetry strategies
    Phonemic, literal, metrical, poetry into prose, rhymed, blank verse, interpretation (version/imitation).
  20. Holmes' four verse-form approaches
    Mimetic, analogical, organic (content-derivative), extraneous (deviant).
  21. Analogical form
    Using the target culture's equivalent verse form instead of the original.
  22. “Türkçe söyleyen”
    Can Yücel's label for his free, domesticating versions of Shakespeare: imitation.
  23. Halman vs Can Yücel on Shakespeare's sonnets
    Halman closer to the source; Yücel free re-creation.
  24. Culture-specific items (Aixelá)
    Conservation (keep, gloss) vs substitution (localise, generalise, delete).
  25. Dual audience
    Children's books address both children and adults (who buy, approve, read aloud).
  26. Ambivalent texts
    Shavit: children's books read on two levels, for children and adults (e.g. Alice).
  27. Shavit's two conditions for manipulation
    Make the text appropriate/useful for the child; adjust plot, character, language to the child's level.
  28. Why is children's literature translated freely?
    Its peripheral position in the literary polysystem (Shavit).
  29. Klingberg's ‘cultural context adaptation’
    Adding explanations, substituting local equivalents, deleting, modernising, purifying, abridging.
  30. Purification
    Removing or softening content considered unsuitable for children (Klingberg).
  31. Oittinen's key idea
    Translating for children: dialogic, guided by the translator's child image; illustrations and reading aloud matter.
  32. Implied translator
    O'Sullivan: traces in the text that reveal the translator's assumed reader.
  33. Davies' strategies (Harry Potter)
    Preservation, addition, omission, globalisation, localisation, transformation, creation.
  34. Biggest problem in translating Alice
    Puns, nonsense and parodies of poems the target children don't know.
  35. Take-home project due date
    Nov 2 (10%).

Translation // Quiz

  1. Dryden's ‘imitation’ means…
    1. word-for-word translation
    2. sense-for-sense translation
    3. free re-creation that may change words and sense
    4. translation into another medium
    Answer: C. Metaphrase → paraphrase → imitation.
  2. Jakobson's ‘intersemiotic’ translation is…
    1. translation between two languages
    2. rewording in the same language
    3. translation into another sign system, like film
    4. machine translation
    Answer: C. Also called transmutation.
  3. ‘Same effect on the new reader’ is Nida's…
    1. formal equivalence
    2. dynamic equivalence
    3. foreignization
    4. skopos
    Answer: B. Reader-oriented.
  4. Venuti argues that fluent domesticating translations make the translator…
    1. famous
    2. invisible
    3. a co-author
    4. unnecessary
    Answer: B. The Translator's Invisibility (1995).
  5. Skopos theory says method depends on…
    1. the author's intention
    2. the purpose of the translation
    3. the source language
    4. word count
    Answer: B. Vermeer, Reiss.
  6. Which is NOT one of Lefevere's seven poetry strategies?
    1. rhymed translation
    2. blank verse translation
    3. calque translation
    4. poetry into prose
    Answer: C. Calque is Vinay & Darbelnet.
  7. Using the target culture's equivalent verse form is Holmes'…
    1. mimetic form
    2. analogical form
    3. organic form
    4. extraneous form
    Answer: B. Mimetic copies the original form.
  8. Can Yücel's “Türkçe söyleyen” Shakespeare is best described as…
    1. metaphrase
    2. foreignizing
    3. imitation / domestication
    4. phonemic translation
    Answer: C. Free re-creation in a Turkish voice.
  9. According to Shavit, children's literature is translated freely because it is…
    1. central in the polysystem
    2. peripheral in the polysystem
    3. short
    4. always illustrated
    Answer: B. Even-Zohar's model applied.
  10. Klingberg's ‘purification’ means…
    1. correcting grammar
    2. removing content judged unsuitable for children
    3. translating names
    4. adding illustrations
    Answer: B. One kind of cultural context adaptation.
  11. Oittinen stresses that translators work for…
    1. the author
    2. their image of the child
    3. the publisher only
    4. literal accuracy
    Answer: B. Translating for Children (2000).
  12. Recreating a lost pun in a different place is called…
    1. modulation
    2. compensation
    3. borrowing
    4. omission
    Answer: B. Hervey & Higgins' term.
  13. Books that work for both children and adults are, for Shavit,…
    1. ambivalent texts
    2. dual texts
    3. crossover poems
    4. skopos texts
    Answer: A. Alice is the classic case.
  14. Replacing ‘Christmas pudding’ with a local dessert is…
    1. preservation
    2. localisation / substitution
    3. calque
    4. foreignization
    Answer: B. Davies' localisation; Aixelá's substitution.

Translation // Write

Long essay template

  1. Intro (3–4 sentences): context → the key term in the question → your thesis (an argument, not a summary).
  2. Three body paragraphs: point → evidence (short quote or precise scene) → analysis → link back to the question.
  3. Comparing two texts? Compare inside each paragraph.
  4. Conclusion: answer the question, then one wider point.
  5. 40 minutes: 5 plan, 30 write, 5 proofread.

Short-answer template

  1. Define or identify in one sentence.
  2. One specific example from a text.
  3. Why it matters.
  4. Stop at 3–5 sentences.

Translation drills

  1. Tyger Tyger, burning bright, / In the forests of the night (Blake, 1794)
    Problem: sound, meter and archaic spelling.
    • Trochaic tetrameter, rhyme (bright/night), alliteration (burning bright, forests).
    • ‘Tyger’ spelling: archaic and mysterious. Turkish ‘Kaplan’ loses it.
    • Choose: rhymed (Lefevere) vs blank verse; keep the incantation even if words change.
    • Compensate with Turkish alliteration or internal rhyme.
  2. How doth the little crocodile / Improve his shining tail (Carroll, 1865)
    Problem: parody of a poem the target readers don't know.
    • Parodies Isaac Watts' ‘How doth the little busy bee’, which every Victorian child memorised.
    • Literal translation keeps the words but kills the joke.
    • Option: parody a moral poem Turkish children know (domestication / creation).
    • Shavit: an ambivalent text, with a joke for adults too.
  3. Twinkle, twinkle, little bat! / How I wonder what you're at! (Carroll)
    Problem: parody + nursery-rhyme rhythm.
    • Parody of Jane Taylor's ‘Twinkle, twinkle, little star’.
    • The original song is widely known in Turkish too, so a parody of the Turkish version can work.
    • Keep the rhythm for reading aloud (Oittinen).
  4. “Mine is a long and a sad tale!” said the Mouse. “It is a long tail, certainly,” said Alice. (Carroll)
    Problem: homophone pun (tale/tail).
    • No Turkish word means both ‘story’ and ‘tail’.
    • Options: footnote (kills humour), substitute another pun, compensate elsewhere.
    • The famous tail-shaped poem that follows needs visual layout too (picture–text link).
  5. Humpty Dumpty sat on a wall, / Humpty Dumpty had a great fall.
    Problem: name, rhyme, rhythm, culture.
    • Meaningless sound-name: keep it (it's known) or invent a Turkish sound-name.
    • Rhyme wall/fall and bouncing rhythm matter more than literal sense.
    • Read-aloud function decides (Oittinen).
  6. Mrs. Tiggy-Winkle (Beatrix Potter, 1905): a hedgehog washerwoman.
    Problem: meaningful/funny name.
    • A playful sound-name that fits the character's look and job.
    • Options: preserve, translate the meaning, invent a Turkish name with the same feel (Davies: creation).
    • Illustration of a hedgehog must still match the name.
  7. They ate Christmas pudding by the fire on Boxing Day.
    Problem: culture-specific items.
    • Preserve (foreignize; maybe gloss) or localise (domesticate).
    • Klingberg: substitution erases the culture; Oittinen: the child must understand.
    • Aixelá / Davies strategies; decide by purpose and age.
  8. Gel gör beni aşk neyledi (Yunus Emre, 13th c.): into English.
    Problem: Sufi vocabulary, refrain, folk meter.
    • Aşk = divine love, not romance: ‘love’ alone flattens it.
    • Refrain and syllabic folk rhythm are hard to copy in English.
    • Options: annotate (foreignizing) or find an English devotional register (analogical).
  9. Shall I compare thee to a summer's day? (Sonnet 18): into Turkish.
    Problem: form + archaic register + ‘summer’.
    • Mimetic form (keep the sonnet) vs organic form.
    • ‘Thee’: Turkish sen/siz choice sets the intimacy.
    • An English summer is mild and short; a Turkish summer is scorching: cultural connotation shifts.
    • Halman (closer) vs Can Yücel (free imitation).

Short answers (model answers)

  1. Explain Dryden's three types of translation.
    In his 1680 preface to Ovid's Epistles, Dryden distinguishes metaphrase (word-for-word, line-by-line translation), paraphrase (translation with latitude: keeping the sense but not the exact words) and imitation (a free re-creation in which the translator may abandon both words and sense). He preferred paraphrase.
  2. What is the difference between domestication and foreignization?
    Venuti's terms (from Schleiermacher). Domestication makes the translation fluent and familiar to target readers, bringing the author to the reader and hiding the translator. Foreignization keeps the source's foreign features visible, bringing the reader to the author. Example: localising a food name vs keeping it with a note.
  3. Why does Shavit say children's literature is translated more freely?
    Because children's literature occupies a peripheral position in the literary polysystem, translators can manipulate it, provided they make the text appropriate and educationally useful for children and adjust plot, characters and language to children's assumed level of understanding.
  4. What is compensation? Give an example.
    Making up for a loss in one place by recreating a similar effect elsewhere. If an English pun can't survive in Turkish at that point, the translator creates a Turkish pun in a nearby sentence, so the text keeps its playful tone overall.
  5. Name Lefevere's seven strategies for translating poetry.
    Phonemic translation, literal translation, metrical translation, poetry into prose, rhymed translation, blank verse translation, and interpretation (version and imitation). Each preserves one feature of the poem at the cost of others.
  6. What is purification in children's literature translation?
    Klingberg's term for removing or softening content adults think unsuitable for children (violence, death, rudeness, sexuality, sometimes religion). It shows how translation reflects the target culture's ideas about childhood and morality.

Essay questions with battle plans

  1. Domestication or foreignization? Discuss with examples from poetry translation.
    1. Thesis: neither is ‘right’; the choice depends on purpose (skopos) and what the translator wants the reader to experience.
    2. Define: Schleiermacher's two directions → Venuti's terms; invisibility.
    3. Poetry: Can Yücel's “Türkçe söyleyen” (domesticating imitation) vs Halman's closer versions.
    4. Lefevere/Holmes: rhymed vs blank verse; mimetic vs analogical form.
    5. Losses and gains: form vs voice; compensation.
    6. Conclusion: a position with a reason (audience, purpose, ethics of the foreign).
  2. Is poetry translatable?
    1. Thesis: poetry is untranslatable as an identical copy but translatable as creative transposition.
    2. Jakobson: untranslatable; only creative transposition.
    3. What resists: sound, meter, rhyme, ambiguity, cultural reference.
    4. Strategies: Lefevere's seven; Dryden's three; Holmes' four.
    5. Example: a sonnet into Turkish or a Yunus Emre ilahi into English.
    6. Conclusion: translation as a new poem in dialogue with the old.
  3. Should children's literature be adapted for the target culture?
    1. Thesis: some adaptation is necessary for readability, but heavy manipulation underestimates children and erases other cultures.
    2. Why it happens: Shavit (peripheral position, didactic norms), dual audience, gatekeepers.
    3. Against: Klingberg (purification, modernisation, deletion).
    4. For the child reader: Oittinen (dialogic, read-aloud, illustrations).
    5. Example: names, food, puns in Alice or Harry Potter (Davies' strategies).
    6. Conclusion: a balanced strategy and a clear purpose.
  4. What are the main challenges of translating wordplay and nonsense in children's books?
    1. Define the problem: puns, invented words, parodies tied to one language and culture.
    2. Examples: Carroll's tale/tail pun; parodies of Watts and Jane Taylor.
    3. Options: literal + footnote (foreignizing, kills the joke), substitution (new pun), omission, compensation.
    4. Theory: Shavit's ambivalent texts; Oittinen's child reader; Davies' creation/transformation.
    5. Conclusion: keep the function (laughter), not the words.

How to beat this exam

  • Her handouts (‘The Victorian Age’ and ‘Victorian Literature’) are now in Intel as two extra context units. ‘The Victorian Age’ ends with three discussion topics: what ‘Victorian’ connotes, the big social and industrial transformations, and whether writers shared the age's optimism. Victorian // Intel

W1–2The Victorian era: historical and cultural context

1837–1901: Britain becomes the first industrial, urban, imperial superpower, and its literature can't stop worrying about what that costs. Learn the dates and buzzwords; they're your context paragraphs.

Timeline

YearEvent
1832First Reform Act: more middle-class men get the vote. Workers don't.
1833Factory Act: limits child labour in textile mills. Slavery abolished in the British Empire.
1834New Poor Law: relief only inside harsh workhouses.
1837Victoria becomes queen.
1838–48Chartism: workers demand the vote through the People's Charter. Petitions rejected (1839, 1842, 1848).
1840sThe ‘Hungry Forties’: depression, unemployment. 1842 Mines Act (no women or children underground). 1844 & 1847 Factory Acts (Ten Hours Act).
1845–52Irish Famine. Mass migration to English cities (Manchester's ‘Little Ireland’).
1846Repeal of the Corn Laws (cheaper bread, free trade).
1848Revolutions across Europe; Marx and Engels' Communist Manifesto; last great Chartist petition.
1851The Great Exhibition at the Crystal Palace: industrial pride on display.
1859Darwin, On the Origin of Species. Religious doubt grows.
1867 / 1884Second and Third Reform Acts: many working men get the vote.
1870s–1901Married Women's Property Acts (1870, 1882); peak of Empire; Victoria dies 1901.

Keywords

  • The ‘Condition of England’ question (Thomas Carlyle): what has industrialisation done to the poor? Carlyle attacked the ‘cash nexus’, the idea that payment is the only bond between people.
  • Utilitarianism (Bentham, J. S. Mill): the greatest happiness of the greatest number, measured and calculated. Dickens' target in Hard Times.
  • Laissez-faire political economy (Adam Smith, Malthus, Ricardo): the market should run itself; wages follow supply and demand.
  • The Woman Question: women's education, work, legal rights, marriage. The ideal of the ‘Angel in the House’ (Coventry Patmore's poem, 1854) and separate spheres (men public, women domestic). J. S. Mill, The Subjection of Women (1869).
  • Evangelicalism and religious doubt; respectability; the work ethic.
  • Empire: wealth from colonies (Jamaica, India) quietly funds English comfort, as in Jane Eyre.

How Victorian fiction worked

  • Serialisation: novels came out in weekly or monthly parts (Dickens' Household Words and All the Year Round). Hence cliffhangers, big casts, recurring catchphrases.
  • Circulating libraries (Mudie's) and the three-volume novel: moral respectability required.
  • Realism: ordinary people, detailed social settings, moral consequences. Plus melodrama, gothic and sentiment mixed in.
  • The social-problem / ‘Condition of England’ / industrial novel: Gaskell's Mary Barton, Dickens' Hard Times, Disraeli's Sybil.

Background (her handout)

  • Britain becomes Europe's most stable and prosperous country: industrial revolution, the railway age, steam in mines, factories and ships; small towns swell into smoky manufacturing centres.
  • But government and Parliament still belong to the privileged few, born rich or newly rich from commerce.
  • England is still mostly agricultural, and country society is still effectively feudal: the landlord rules; only the parson (and maybe the apothecary or surgeon) has any other authority.
  • For the poor in the new towns, industry brings dirt, squalor, ugliness and crime: labourers with no redress, women underpaid, children overworked in terrible conditions.

Queen Victoria and the Empire (her second handout)

  • Victoria reigned 1837–1901 (her handout says she was ‘made queen’ in 1838, the coronation year): about 63 years, the longest reign up to then. Her first Prime Minister, Lord Melbourne, taught her politics; Disraeli is the other famous PM. Much of the age's success was really theirs.
  • Prince Albert died in 1861; she mourned in black and withdrew for about ten years. Her strict, puritan sense of duty and discipline matched the national mood.
  • Shows of power: the Great Exhibition (1851) in the Crystal Palace, the Golden Jubilee (1887), the Diamond Jubilee (1897).
  • Wars: the Opium War (1839–42), after which Britain gets Hong Kong; the Crimean War (1853–56), Britain allied with the Ottoman Empire against Russia; the Boer War (1899–1902) in South Africa, called the first ‘total’ war.
  • India passes from the East India Company to the Crown in 1858; Victoria becomes Empress of India in 1876. Egypt and the Suez Canal follow. Slogans: ‘the sun never sets on the British Empire’, Britain as ‘the workshop of the world’.
  • ‘Grandmother of Europe’: her children and grandchildren married into Europe's royal families (Kaiser Wilhelm II was her grandson). Lake Victoria, Victoria Falls, and states and cities in Australia and Canada are named after her.
What they’ll askDon't write a history essay. Two precise context facts per answer (e.g. ‘after the 1834 Poor Law’, ‘in the Chartist 1840s’) beat a page of general history.
W1–2Industry, class, women and the Chartists (her handout)

The Industrial Revolution makes Britain the richest country on earth and the first to find out what mass urban poverty looks like. Her handout walks through transport, towns, the middle class, women and the Chartists, and keeps pointing at the novels that show it.

The Industrial Revolution

  • A process from the mid-18th century lasting more than a century. Britain becomes the richest country in the world, and the first to face the social problems of fast urban industry.
  • Transport: turnpikes (toll barriers, late 17th c.) make road users pay for the roads; Macadam (broken-stone surfaces) and Telford (roads and bridges) give England the best roads in Europe; the Duke of Bridgewater's canals; then the steam railway: cheaper, wider travel, a more uniform national culture, and above all migration from the countryside into the towns.
  • Agricultural Revolution: profitable new farming needs capital and enclosure; small farmers sell up and emigrate to the colonies or drift to the industrial towns.
  • Inventions: steam power (Watt), the battery (Volta), the textile mill (Cartwright); railways spread in the 1830s–40s.
  • The economy grows from 1846 with Free Trade; low wages make exports competitive. Three pillars: coal, iron, cotton.

The biggest social change in English history

  • After the long war with France (1793–1815) Britain is a great power and the world's leading economy: the first urban, industrial society. Its paradox: new wealth next to a new kind of urban poverty.
  • 1750–1850: masses move from country to town. Small farmers and rural craftsmen become an urban proletariat; factory owners become a new employing class.
  • It hits the North and the Midlands far more than the South: the industrial North pushes against the conservative South. In novels: Gaskell's North and South, Eliot's Silas Marner, Dickens' Bleak House; old rural life vs modernity in Hardy's Tess of the d'Urbervilles and The Mayor of Casterbridge.
  • Towns grow with no care for dignity or welfare, ‘jungles’ where the law is survival of the fittest; women and children exploited in factories. In novels: Mary Barton, Oliver Twist, David Copperfield, Hard Times.

Manchester and the Chartists (her version)

  • Peterloo, 1819: about 60,000 unemployed weavers and families at St Peter's Fields, Manchester, to hear ‘Orator’ Hunt. The Hussars charge: 11 dead, more than 400 injured. The government's reputation is wrecked.
  • Manchester, the textile capital, trebles in size. Life expectancy: a Manchester labourer 17, a farm labourer 38. Over half of labourers' children die before five. In ‘Little Ireland’: no water, no sewers, back-to-back houses, straw beds, families sharing corners of one room.
  • 1832 Reform Act: the vote for men with property worth £10 a year in rent: the middle and lower middle class. Workers still have no voice.
  • The People's Charter (London Working Men's Association; presented to Parliament in 1839 by Thomas Attwood): votes for all men and no property qualification for MPs. Rejected with howls of derision in 1839, and again in 1842. Meanwhile bread prices climb, 10,000 Manchester weavers lose their jobs, and the Irish potato blight sends migrants into the North-West.
  • 1848: revolutions across Europe. Chartist MP Feargus O'Connor (elected in Nottingham) brings the Charter a third time; a crowd of 15,000–100,000 gathers at Kennington Common. London barricades itself, defended by the Duke of Wellington. O'Connor loses his nerve, rides to Parliament in three cabs, and the soaked crowd drifts away in the rain. Rejected for the last time.
  • Why it failed (her verdict): isolation from the middle class. Trade unions, better harvests and the Anti-Corn Law League took over. But Marx and Engels' Communist Manifesto (1848) used Manchester's factories as its example.

Votes, free trade and the working class

  • The old electoral system: new industrial cities had no MPs, while ‘rotten boroughs’ (nearly empty places) elected the local squire's man.
  • 1846: Repeal of the Corn Laws (taxes on imported corn that kept bread dear): the government admits Britain is industrial, not agricultural, gives workers cheap food, and sides with the middle class against the landowners. A turning point.
  • Mining and metal workers form a working-class aristocracy → the Trades Union Congress (1868). 1867: Disraeli's Second Reform Act gives urban workers the vote; 1870: Forster's Act, universal primary education; 1884: agricultural workers vote; by 1900 the Labour Party.
  • Novels that track all this: George Eliot (who campaigned for secular education and trade unions) and Gaskell.

Women's changing role

  • 18th century: the Bluestockings, women intellectuals around Mrs Montagu. Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792), demands education for women, not recognised until the Education Acts of 1870 and 1902.
  • More girls' boarding schools (Miss Pinkerton's Academy in Thackeray's Vanity Fair).
  • The catch: Puritan, middle-class morality made marriage sacred and denied women's sensuality: the belief that ‘a good woman does not have sexual desire’. Upper-class Fielding's ‘natural’ women vs Richardson's idealised ones; in the 19th century the Richardsonian view wins.
  • Strong women open closed professions: writers, journalists, nurses. Factory work gives a low-level economic independence.
  • Married Women's Property Acts end the husband's control over his wife's money (her handout: 1882 and 1892; the main Acts were 1870 and 1882). The vote: women over 30 in 1918, equal terms at 21 in 1928 (her handout says 1939: wrong).

The middle class

  • Rich and growing thanks to industry, but at first politically underprivileged: the system favoured landed society. They fought and won representation in the first half of the century.
  • They are the class in the novels and the class the novels were written for, so novelists satirise money-worship: the nouveau-riche Mr Osborne (Vanity Fair, 1848), Podsnap (Our Mutual Friend, 1865).
  • Below them, a huge lower middle class of small traders, created by the new consumer society: the most fluid class, politically unstable, often decisive in elections, and leaders of the Labour movement. It fills the novels of Dickens and H. G. Wells.
What they’ll askHer handout ends with discussion topics: the connotations of ‘Victorian’, the main social and industrial transformations, and whether writers shared the optimism of economic growth. All three essay plans are first in Write.
W1–2Victorian literature at a glance (her handouts)

The novel is king, women write half the good ones under men's names, science shakes everybody's faith, and Carlyle tells writers to go and look at the poor. One page for every ‘who wrote what, when’ question.

Why the novel

  • In the Romantic period poetry dominated; in the Victorian period, the novel. The English became ‘a nation of avid novel-readers’; the theatre was considered disreputable.
  • Why: a growing, moneyed, educated middle-class reading public and more circulating libraries.
  • Serialisation strained writers artistically, but many major novels (Dickens, Thackeray, Hardy) first appeared in parts.
  • Women had already proved themselves: Ann Radcliffe, Fanny Burney, Maria Edgeworth, Jane Austen.

Two phases, and what broke the confidence

  • Early Victorian novelists identified with their age: they accepted progress without much question; the age was the triumph of Protestantism; frank writing about sex became taboo (‘Fielding was banished’).
  • Later novelists questioned, criticised and turned hostile to the age's assumptions.
  • Science did much of it: Lyell, Principles of Geology (1830–33); Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1859) and The Descent of Man (1871). The universe looked constantly changing and governed by chance, not stable and clear. Many intellectuals lost their faith or built a private, untheological religion.
  • Hume's scepticism provoked Kant's answer. Thomas Carlyle (1795–1881) brought German thought (Goethe above all) to Britain: reform, self-fulfilment, ‘hero worship’, and an attack on laissez-faire and on the utilitarianism of Bentham and J. S. Mill. He inspired the ‘social problem’ novels of 1830–60: Gaskell, Disraeli, Dickens.

The novelists

WriterWhat to know
Charles Dickens (1812–70)First novel The Pickwick Papers (1836), last Our Mutual Friend (1864–65); Oliver Twist, Dombey and Son, Bleak House, Little Dorrit, Great Expectations. Popular entertainment plus social criticism, growing darker over time.
William Thackeray (1811–63)Dickens' rival: sharper, more detached satire, a more middle-class world. Vanity Fair (1848), ‘A Novel without a Hero’, a historical novel about recent history.
Charlotte Brontë (1816–55)Jane Eyre (1847), with gothic themes.
Emily Brontë (1818–48)Wuthering Heights (1847), her only novel: Gothic Romanticism from a woman's point of view (class, myth, gender).
Anne Brontë (1820–49)The Tenant of Wildfell Hall (1848): realist, often called the first sustained feminist novel.
George Eliot (Mary Ann Evans, 1819–80)The Mill on the Floss (1860), Middlemarch (1872), Silas Marner. Like the Brontës, a male pseudonym.
Elizabeth Gaskell (1810–65)Mary Barton (1848), Cranford (1853), North and South (1855).
Thomas Hardy (1840–1928)The major late novelist: Under the Greenwood Tree (1872), Far from the Madding Crowd (1874), The Mayor of Casterbridge (1886), Tess of the d'Urbervilles (1891), Jude the Obscure (1895).
OthersAnthony Trollope, George Meredith, George Gissing, Samuel Butler, Wilkie Collins.

The typical Victorian novel

  • Idealised portraits of hard lives in which hard work, perseverance, love and luck win out; virtue is rewarded and wrongdoers punished; an improving story with a moral lesson at its heart.
  • The formula gets more complicated as the century goes on (Hardy is the obvious case).

Poetry, drama, and everything else

  • Tennyson (Poet Laureate for over 40 years) and Robert Browning were the famous poets; Elizabeth Barrett Browning and Robert carried on their love affair in verse. Tennyson's ‘The Charge of the Light Brigade’ attacks a military blunder: the establishment criticising the establishment.
  • Matthew Arnold; Gerard Manley Hopkins (published only in 1918, inspired by Old English verse); the Pre-Raphaelites: Dante Gabriel Rossetti and his sister Christina (now rated the stronger poet).
  • Reclaiming the past: Tennyson's Idylls of the King (Arthurian stories from Malory) to spread chivalrous ideals at home and across the Empire.
  • Drama only matters late: Gilbert and Sullivan (from the 1870s), Shaw (1890s), Wilde's The Importance of Being Earnest (1895).
  • Children's literature: the Victorians ‘invented childhood’ (child-labour laws, compulsory school): Lewis Carroll, Anna Sewell, Tom Brown's Schooldays.
  • Non-fiction: Darwin; J. S. Mill (logic, liberty, utilitarianism); Carlyle (The French Revolution, On Heroes and Hero-Worship); Macaulay's History of England; Engels, The Condition of the Working Class in England; William Morris, News from Nowhere; the Oxford English Dictionary begins.
  • Gothic and the fantastic: Sherlock Holmes, Dracula, Jekyll and Hyde: monsters that walk into London.
What they’ll askClassic short answers: ‘Why did the novel dominate?’, ‘What shook Victorian confidence?’ (Lyell, Darwin), ‘Who was Carlyle and why does he matter to the social-problem novel?’, ‘What was the typical Victorian novel formula?’
W3Romanticism vs Realism: Austen, Sense and Sensibility (1811)

Pre-Victorian, but it's the bridge. Two sisters: Elinor (sense: self-control) and Marianne (sensibility: Romantic feeling). Marianne nearly dies of feeling too much. Behind the love plots, it's a novel about money.

Romanticism vs Realism

Romanticism (c. 1798–1830s)Realism (Victorian mainstream)
Emotion, imagination, the individualSocial life, moral consequences, community
Nature, the sublime, the picturesqueTowns, drawing rooms, factories, money
The exceptional hero or poetOrdinary, middle-class people
Wordsworth, Coleridge, Byron, Shelley, KeatsDickens, Gaskell, Eliot, Trollope (Austen as a forerunner)

Plot

  • Mr Dashwood dies; Norland Park goes to his son John Dashwood. John promises to help his stepmother and half-sisters, but his wife Fanny talks him down from £3,000 to practically nothing (the famous chapter 2).
  • Mrs Dashwood, Elinor, Marianne and young Margaret move to Barton Cottage in Devonshire, a gift from cousin Sir John Middleton. Busybody Mrs Jennings is his mother-in-law.
  • Elinor loves Edward Ferrars (Fanny's brother), who is quiet and secretly engaged to the scheming Lucy Steele. Lucy tells Elinor in confidence; Elinor suffers in silence.
  • Marianne twists her ankle in the rain and is rescued by dashing Willoughby, who shares her taste for poetry. They act like an engaged couple (he cuts a lock of her hair), then he leaves suddenly.
  • In London, Willoughby snubs Marianne and marries the rich Miss Grey. We learn he seduced and abandoned Eliza, the ward of the older, steady Colonel Brandon.
  • Marianne falls dangerously ill at Cleveland after walking in wet grass. Willoughby turns up and confesses to Elinor: he did love Marianne but chose money.
  • Edward's engagement comes out; his mother disinherits him; Lucy switches to his brother Robert, who got the money. Edward is free and marries Elinor, taking the parish of Delaford from Brandon. Marianne, wiser, marries Brandon.

Themes

  • Sense vs sensibility: not a simple opposition. Elinor feels deeply but controls it; Marianne learns restraint. The novel argues for a balance.
  • Money and marriage: inheritance through the male line leaves women poor; marriage is women's only economic future. Willoughby and Lucy both pick money over love.
  • Women's dependence: the Dashwood women's fate depends on a brother's kindness and a cousin's charity.
  • Privacy and propriety: secrets (Lucy's engagement, Eliza's story) and the social cost of showing feelings.

Technique

  • Free indirect discourse: the narrator slips into a character's thoughts (mostly Elinor's), so we judge through her.
  • Irony: the money-talk in chapter 2 is pure comic irony.
  • Satire of Romantic sensibility: Marianne's cult of feeling, the picturesque, dead leaves.

Ammo: lines to quote

Elinor… possessed a strength of understanding, and coolness of judgment
Ch. 1 · Sense defined.
She was sensible and clever; but eager in everything: her sorrows, her joys, could have no moderation.
Ch. 1, on Marianne · Sensibility defined.
What they’ll askWhy is a 1811 novel on a Victorian syllabus? Answer: it shows the move from Romantic feeling to realist social judgement, and it sets up the Victorian ‘Woman Question’ (inheritance, marriage, dependence).
W4Gender and the Woman Question: Charlotte Brontë, Jane Eyre (1847)

A poor, plain orphan governess insists she has a soul equal to any man's, refuses to be anyone's mistress, and comes back only when she has money and he has been cut down to size. Meanwhile there's a woman locked in the attic, which critics have been arguing about ever since.

Basics

  • Published 1847 under the male pseudonym ‘Currer Bell’; subtitled An Autobiography. First-person, told by the older Jane looking back.
  • A Bildungsroman (growth story) in five places: Gateshead → Lowood → Thornfield → Moor House → Ferndean. Gothic elements (red-room, attic, fire, mysterious laughter).

Plot by place

  • Gateshead: orphan Jane lives with her cruel aunt Mrs Reed and bullying cousin John Reed. Locked in the red-room where her uncle died, she sees a light, panics, and faints. Sent away to school.
  • Lowood: charity school run by the hypocritical Evangelical Mr Brocklehurst (starves the girls, preaches humility while his family wears silk). Jane's friend Helen Burns preaches Christian endurance and dies of consumption; kind Miss Temple is the teacher. Jane stays eight years (six as pupil, two as teacher).
  • Thornfield: governess to Adèle, ward of Mr Rochester. They meet when his horse slips on ice. Strange laughter (blamed on Grace Poole); Jane saves Rochester from a fire in his bed. He courts the beautiful Blanche Ingram to make Jane jealous; disguises himself as a gypsy fortune-teller; Mason is attacked at night. Rochester proposes under the chestnut tree, which lightning splits that night.
  • The wedding is stopped: Rochester is already married to Bertha Mason, a Creole woman from Jamaica, ‘mad’ and locked in the attic. Rochester asks Jane to live with him anyway. She refuses and flees with nothing.
  • Moor House: starving, she's taken in by St John Rivers and his sisters Diana and Mary, who turn out to be her cousins. She inherits £20,000 from her uncle in Madeira and shares it equally among the four. St John, a cold missionary, proposes a loveless marriage to go to India. On the point of accepting, she hears Rochester's voice calling her name.
  • Ferndean: Thornfield has burned down; Bertha set the fire and jumped from the roof. Rochester is blind and has lost a hand. ‘Reader, I married him.’ He later recovers some sight and sees their first son.

Themes

  • Gender and the Woman Question: Jane demands equal feeling, work and dignity for women (the ch. 12 rooftop speech).
  • Class: the governess is neither servant nor lady. Jane only marries Rochester once she is financially independent and he is humbled: equality before marriage.
  • Passion vs principle: she loves Rochester but won't be his mistress; she respects St John but won't marry without love. She rejects both extremes.
  • Religion: three models: Brocklehurst (hypocrisy), Helen (patient endurance), St John (ambitious self-sacrifice). Jane finds her own.
  • Empire: Bertha from Jamaica, the uncle's money from Madeira, St John's India. Colonial wealth and colonial ‘others’ underwrite the happy ending.

Critics to name

  • *Gilbert & Gubar, The Madwoman in the Attic (1979)*: Bertha is Jane's dark double, the rage a Victorian woman must lock away.
  • *Jean Rhys, Wide Sargasso Sea (1966)*: a postcolonial rewriting that gives Bertha (Antoinette) her own story.
  • Gayatri Spivak (1985): the novel's feminist individualism depends on silencing the colonial woman.

Devices

  • First-person retrospective narration and direct addresses to the reader.
  • Fire and ice imagery (passion vs coldness: St John is ice); the red-room (imprisonment, anger); birds (freedom, captivity); the split chestnut tree (omen).
  • Doubling: Jane / Bertha; Rochester / St John.

Ammo: lines to quote

Women are supposed to be very calm generally: but women feel just as men feel
Ch. 12 · The Woman Question in one line.
Do you think, because I am poor, obscure, plain, and little, I am soulless and heartless? You think wrong!
Ch. 23 · Equality of souls across class and gender.
I am no bird; and no net ensnares me: I am a free human being with an independent will
Ch. 23 · Autonomy; bird imagery.
I care for myself. The more solitary, the more friendless, the more unsustained I am, the more I will respect myself.
Ch. 27 · Principle over passion: she leaves.
Reader, I married him.
Ch. 38 · Jane is the subject of the sentence: she married him.
What they’ll askThe week title is ‘Gender & the Woman Question’. Expected essay: ‘How does Jane Eyre engage with the position of women?’ Use the ch. 12 and ch. 23 speeches, the governess's class position, and Bertha as a complication.
W5Class, work, child labour: Dickens, Hard Times (1854) + EBB, “The Cry of the Children” (1843)

Dickens attacks a philosophy (Utilitarian ‘Facts’) that treats children as empty containers and workers as ‘Hands’. Barrett Browning attacks the same system in verse, through children working in mines and mills. Both are protest literature.

Hard Times: basics

  • Serialised weekly in Dickens' magazine Household Words (1854); dedicated to Thomas Carlyle. Short, a ‘moral fable’ (F. R. Leavis).
  • Set in Coketown, a fictional northern mill town (modelled partly on Preston, where there was a big strike in 1853–54).
  • Three books with farming titles: ‘Sowing’, ‘Reaping’, ‘Garnering’. Gradgrind sows Facts and reaps disaster.

Who's who

  • Thomas Gradgrind: retired merchant, MP, Utilitarian; raises his children on Facts only. Changes at the end.
  • Louisa Gradgrind: his daughter; emotionally starved; marries Bounderby out of duty; nearly runs off with Harthouse.
  • Tom Gradgrind (‘the whelp’): selfish son; robs Bounderby's bank and frames Stephen.
  • Josiah Bounderby: mill owner and banker, ‘the Bully of humility’; boasts he was abandoned in a ditch and rose alone. A lie: his loving mother, Mrs Pegler, raised him.
  • Sissy Jupe: circus girl (‘girl number twenty’); can't define a horse; full of kindness. The novel's heart.
  • Bitzer: model pupil; defines a horse perfectly; grows into pure self-interest.
  • Stephen Blackpool: honest power-loom weaver; trapped in marriage to a drunken wife (divorce is only for the rich); loves Rachael; refuses to join the union because of a promise, is shunned by workers and sacked by Bounderby; framed; falls into the Old Hell Shaft and dies. ‘It's aw a muddle.’
  • Slackbridge: loud union agitator (Dickens is suspicious of unions). James Harthouse: bored gentleman who tempts Louisa. Mrs Sparsit: Bounderby's snobbish housekeeper, spying on Louisa (her imagined ‘staircase’). Mr Sleary: lisping circus owner: ‘People mutht be amuthed.’

Plot

  • Gradgrind's school: Sissy can't define a horse; Bitzer can. Sissy's father vanishes; Gradgrind takes her in.
  • Louisa marries Bounderby (30 years older), to help Tom. Stephen asks Bounderby about divorce; refused. He won't join the union, is shunned, then fired.
  • Tom robs the bank and casts suspicion on Stephen, who has left town. Harthouse tempts Louisa; she flees to her father and collapses: his system has left her empty.
  • Rachael and Sissy find Stephen dying in the Old Hell Shaft. Tom is exposed; Bitzer tries to arrest him for advancement; the circus helps Tom escape abroad. Bounderby is exposed by Mrs Pegler and dies later in a fit; Gradgrind reforms.

Themes

  • Fact vs Fancy: Utilitarian education kills imagination, feeling and moral sense. The circus = fancy, play, compassion.
  • Industrial capitalism and class: workers reduced to ‘Hands’ (metonymy); Bounderby's self-made-man myth.
  • Education: children as ‘little vessels’ to be filled with facts.
  • Marriage and divorce law: Stephen's trap; Louisa's loveless marriage.
  • Dickens' limits: sympathetic to workers but distrusts unions (Slackbridge) and offers moral, not political, solutions.

“The Cry of the Children” (Elizabeth Barrett Browning, 1843)

  • Inspired by R. H. Horne's report for the Children's Employment Commission (1842–43) on children in mines and factories.
  • Epigraph from Euripides' Medea: a mother asking her children why they look at her. Children as victims of their own society.
  • The children weep while lambs bleat and birds sing: nature's playtime vs their work. They'd rather die; little Alice is happy in her grave.
  • In the factories, the iron wheels turn all day and the children's heads and hearts turn with them. Machine rhythm in long, heavy lines and repetition.
  • They can't pray: they only know the words ‘Our Father’, and God seems as distant as their masters. Religion has failed them too.
  • Ends by turning on the nation: the child's sob ‘curses deeper’ than a strong man's anger.
  • Devices: direct address (‘O my brothers’), refrain-like repetition, contrast with nature, apostrophe to the ‘cruel nation’, accusatory irony (‘the country of the free’).

Pairing them

  • Both attack a system that treats children as instruments: Gradgrind's classroom and the factory wheel.
  • EBB uses pathos and religious outrage; Dickens uses satire and caricature plus a sentimental heart (Sissy, Stephen).
  • Both appeal to middle-class readers' conscience rather than calling for revolution.

Ammo: lines to quote

Now, what I want is, Facts. Teach these boys and girls nothing but Facts. Facts alone are wanted in life.
Gradgrind, Book 1 ch. 1 · Utilitarian education.
Quadruped. Graminivorous. Forty teeth…
Bitzer, Book 1 ch. 2 · Knowledge without understanding.
It was a town of red brick, or of brick that would have been red if the smoke and ashes had allowed it
Book 1 ch. 5 · Coketown: industrial pollution and sameness.
People mutht be amuthed.
Sleary · Fancy as a human need.
How could you give me life, and take from me all the inappreciable things that raise it from the state of conscious death?
Louisa to Gradgrind, Book 2 ch. 12 · The system's failure.
Do ye hear the children weeping, O my brothers, / Ere the sorrow comes with years?
EBB, “The Cry of the Children”, opening · Direct address to readers.
They are weeping in the playtime of the others, / In the country of the free.
EBB, stanza 1 · Irony: free England, enslaved children.
But the child's sob in the silence curses deeper / Than the strong man in his wrath.
EBB, last lines · Moral accusation of the nation.
What they’ll askWeek title: ‘Social Critique: Class, Work, Industrialization, Child Labor and Social Mobility’. Social mobility = Bounderby's fake self-made story and Bitzer's rise through selfishness. Use them.
W6Revolution and sacrifice: Dickens, A Tale of Two Cities (1859)

London and Paris, before and during the French Revolution. Dickens hates the cruelty of the aristocrats and is terrified by the cruelty of the mob. A drunken lawyer gives his life for another man and finally means something.

Basics

  • Serialised weekly in All the Year Round (1859). Historical novel; Dickens' main source was *Carlyle's The French Revolution*** (1837).
  • Three books: ‘Recalled to Life’, ‘The Golden Thread’, ‘The Track of a Storm’.
  • Famous opening built on antithesis: ‘It was the best of times, it was the worst of times…’

Who's who

  • Dr Alexandre Manette: unjustly imprisoned 18 years in the Bastille (cell ‘One Hundred and Five, North Tower’); makes shoes in his trauma.
  • Lucie Manette: his daughter, the ‘golden thread’ binding everyone. Marries Darnay.
  • Charles Darnay: French aristocrat (real name Evrémonde) who renounces his family's title and lives in England.
  • Sydney Carton: brilliant, drunk, self-hating English lawyer; looks exactly like Darnay; loves Lucie hopelessly.
  • Mr Stryver: pushy barrister who takes credit for Carton's work. Jarvis Lorry: loyal banker from Tellson's.
  • Ernest and Madame Defarge: wine-shop owners in Saint Antoine, revolutionaries. Madame Defarge knits a secret register of names to be killed; her family was destroyed by the Evrémondes.
  • Marquis St. Evrémonde: Darnay's cruel uncle; runs over a peasant child and tosses a coin; is murdered by the father, Gaspard.
  • Jerry Cruncher: Tellson's messenger and secret ‘resurrection man’ (grave robber). Miss Pross: Lucie's fierce English nurse.

Plot

  • Book 1: 1775. Lorry and Lucie go to Paris to bring Manette, ‘recalled to life’, back to London.
  • Book 2: Darnay is tried for treason at the Old Bailey; Carton saves him by showing how alike they look. Lucie marries Darnay; Carton promises to give his life for her if needed. In France the Marquis is murdered. 1789: the Bastille is stormed; Defarge searches Manette's old cell. Darnay goes to Paris to help his servant Gabelle.
  • Book 3: Darnay is arrested as an emigrant aristocrat; Manette's fame frees him, but he's re-arrested. At the second trial, a letter Manette wrote in the Bastille is read: it curses the Evrémonde family for their crimes. Darnay is condemned.
  • Carton drugs Darnay, swaps places with him in prison, and goes to the guillotine, comforting a young seamstress. Miss Pross fights Madame Defarge, whose pistol goes off and kills her (Pross goes deaf). Carton's last thoughts: a prophecy of peace and the line about a ‘far, far better thing’.

Themes

  • Resurrection: Manette recalled to life, Darnay saved from death twice, Carton's spiritual rebirth through sacrifice; Cruncher's grave-robbing parodies it.
  • Sacrifice and redemption: Carton.
  • Revolution and violence: sympathy for the oppressed (the Marquis, starving Saint Antoine) and horror at the Terror (La Guillotine, Madame Defarge). Oppression breeds violence: a warning to England about its own poor.
  • Doubles: Carton/Darnay; London/Paris; Lucie/Madame Defarge.
  • Imprisonment: the Bastille, Manette's mind, Carton's wasted life.
  • Fate and history: the past (Manette's letter) returns to condemn the present.

Devices

  • Antithesis and parallelism (the opening). Symbols: knitting, spilled wine in the street (foreshadowing blood), shoemaking, the golden thread, the ‘sea’ of the mob. Foreshadowing and coincidence (serial form).

Ammo: lines to quote

It was the best of times, it was the worst of times
Book 1 ch. 1 · Antithesis; an age of extremes.
Recalled to life.
Book 1 title / Lorry's message · Resurrection theme.
It is a far, far better thing that I do, than I have ever done; it is a far, far better rest that I go to than I have ever known.
Carton, last lines · Sacrifice and redemption.
What they’ll askWeek title: ‘Revolution, Social Injustice, and Sacrifice: The Individual in Times of Revolution’. That's the essay: how do individuals (Carton, Manette, Madame Defarge) act within, against, or because of history?
W7Industrial fiction: Gaskell, Mary Barton (1848) + Engels, The Condition of the Working Class (1845)

Manchester in the hungry 1840s, seen twice: by a minister's wife who wants rich and poor to understand each other (Gaskell), and by a German factory-owner's son who says the system is killing people on purpose (Engels). Taught Nov 6, a week before the exam.

Mary Barton: basics

  • Published anonymously in 1848; subtitle A Tale of Manchester Life. Elizabeth Gaskell was the wife of a Unitarian minister in Manchester and worked among the poor.
  • In her Preface she says she knows nothing of political economy; she writes to give voice to the suffering ‘dumb people’ and to help the classes understand each other.
  • A ‘Condition of England’ / industrial novel. Originally titled John Barton: he's the tragic centre.

Who's who

  • John Barton: mill worker, union man and Chartist. Loses his wife; his son died during unemployment while the mill owners stayed comfortable. Embittered, he takes opium.
  • Mary Barton: his daughter, a dressmaker. Flattered by Harry Carson, but really loves Jem.
  • Jem Wilson: honest engineer who loves Mary.
  • Harry Carson: rich mill owner's son; wants Mary as a mistress; mocks the workers.
  • Mr Carson: his father, mill owner.
  • Esther: Mary's aunt, a ‘fallen woman’ (prostitute) who tries to warn Mary.
  • Job Legh (self-taught naturalist) and his blind granddaughter Margaret; Will Wilson (sailor, Jem's cousin); the Davenports (a family dying of fever in a cellar).

Plot

  • 1839: the Chartist petition is rejected by Parliament; Barton returns from London bitter. The Davenport cellar scene shows starvation and typhus.
  • Mary rejects Jem, hoping to marry Harry Carson and lift her father out of poverty, then realises she loves Jem.
  • During a strike, Harry Carson draws a cruel caricature of the workers' delegation. The union men draw lots to kill him; John Barton draws the lot and shoots him.
  • Jem's gun is found at the scene: Jem is arrested. But the gun's paper wadding is a torn piece of a Valentine with Mary's name on it, which her father had been using to copy a poem. Mary finds the matching piece at home: she knows the truth.
  • To save Jem without betraying her father, Mary chases Will Wilson (Jem's alibi) down the Mersey by boat. Jem is acquitted at the Liverpool trial; Mary collapses.
  • Dying, John Barton confesses to Mr Carson, who at first wants revenge, then (reading the Gospel) forgives him. Barton dies in Carson's arms. Carson starts improving conditions. Mary and Jem emigrate to Canada.

Themes

  • Class conflict and the gulf between masters and men: misunderstanding and indifference, not pure evil.
  • Christian reconciliation: forgiveness and sympathy as the cure (Carson and Barton).
  • Poverty, disease, hunger: realism about Manchester slums.
  • Women's work and sexual danger: Mary as dressmaker, Esther as warning.
  • Limits: the ending sends the young couple abroad. Gaskell can imagine sympathy but not a changed system. Critics like W. R. Greg said she was unfair to the masters.

Engels, The Condition of the Working Class in England (1845)

  • Written in German by Friedrich Engels (24), who was working in his family's cotton firm in Manchester; English translation 1887. Guided round the slums by the Irish worker Mary Burns.
  • Describes the Old Town, the river Irk, ‘Little Ireland’: filth, overcrowding, cellars, disease.
  • Shows how Manchester's layout hides the poor: the main streets are lined with shops, so the middle class can commute through the city without ever seeing a working-class district.
  • Accuses the bourgeoisie of ‘social murder’: society knowingly keeps workers in conditions that kill them early.
  • Predicts that class war and revolution are inevitable. A founding text of Marxism (with Marx he wrote the Communist Manifesto in 1848).

Gaskell vs Engels (what she will ask you)

GaskellEngels
FormNovel: individual stories, feelingSocial investigation: statistics, streets, analysis
Cause of miseryIgnorance and lack of sympathy between classesThe capitalist system itself
SolutionChristian understanding and forgivenessClass struggle, revolution
SharedSame city, same decade, same cellars and fevers; both want middle-class readers to see what's hidden

Gaskell's life (her handout)

  • Born Elizabeth Stevenson, 1810, Chelsea. Her mother died when she was a baby; she grew up with an aunt in Knutsford, Cheshire. Her father was a Unitarian.
  • Her brother John, a sailor with the East India Company, went missing at sea (1827). Compare Peter's disappearance in Cranford.
  • 1832: married William Gaskell, a Unitarian minister in Manchester (a scholar and an authority on Lancashire dialect).
  • Grief over the death of her baby son from scarlet fever, plus her charity work among the poor, drove her to write Mary Barton.
  • Mary Barton (1848) appeared under the pen name ‘Cotton Mather Mills, Esq.’, to protect her husband, who preached to the very mill-owners she criticised. Manchester mill-owners and the Tory press were outraged; Carlyle praised it. She didn't mean it as a political plea, but it was one anyway.
  • Fame: Dickens recruits her for Household Words (→ Cranford, 1853), though she found him too demanding; friendship with Charlotte Brontë, whose Life she wrote (1857).
  • North and South (1855) is often seen as a retreat from Mary Barton's abrasive criticism: middle-class heroes and a clear message of reconciliation between classes, written in a more prosperous 1850s Manchester. Later: Sylvia's Lovers, Cousin Phillis, Wives and Daughters. She died suddenly in 1865, taking tea.
  • Unitarianism: freedom of thought, girls' education, no hostility to women's achievement. It explains a lot about her.

Cranford (1853), briefly

  • Began as separate sketches in Household Words, hence its episodic structure.
  • A town of genteel, ageing ladies too poor to live as they'd like, keeping up appearances: old caps worn indoors and swapped when visitors knock, candles lit only at the last second, everyone pretending to be surprised by cakes they all know the hostess baked.
  • Behind the comedy: a world that ignores the huge economic changes around it but can't escape them. Miss Matty is ruined by a bank failure (country banks collapsed after cash payments, suspended 1797–1817, resumed).
  • Her questions on it: characterisation, plot, theme, point of view; Gaskell's irony about pride and prejudice; narrator Mary Smith's role; Miss Matty's life story; her brother Peter vs Gaskell's own brother; why the bank collapsed; comparison with Austen's Pride and Prejudice.

Ammo: lines to quote

I know nothing of Political Economy, or the theories of trade.
Gaskell, Preface · Her claim to write from feeling, not theory.
What they’ll askHer presentation rubric for non-fiction says: explain how the non-fiction text relates to the literary text: illuminate, complement, complicate, contradict. Use exactly those verbs in your Engels paragraph.

Victorian // Flashcards

Cover the answer, say it out loud, then check.

  1. When did Victoria reign?
    1837–1901.
  2. First Reform Act
    1832: vote extended to more middle-class men, not workers.
  3. New Poor Law
    1834: relief for the poor mainly inside workhouses, made deliberately harsh.
  4. Chartism
    Working-class movement (1838–48) demanding the vote via the People's Charter; petitions rejected 1839, 1842, 1848.
  5. The ‘Condition of England’ question
    Carlyle's phrase: what has industrialisation done to the poor? Gave its name to the social-problem novel.
  6. ‘Cash nexus’
    Carlyle: payment as the only bond between employer and worker.
  7. Utilitarianism
    Bentham/Mill: the greatest happiness of the greatest number. Dickens' target in Hard Times.
  8. The ‘Angel in the House’
    Coventry Patmore's poem (1854); the ideal of the selfless, domestic Victorian wife.
  9. Separate spheres
    Ideology: men in public life and work, women in the home.
  10. Great Exhibition
    1851, Crystal Palace: a showcase of industrial progress.
  11. Serialisation
    Novels published in parts (weekly/monthly), e.g. Hard Times in Household Words.
  12. Sense vs sensibility
    Elinor's self-control vs Marianne's Romantic feeling. Austen argues for balance.
  13. Who gets Norland Park?
    John Dashwood, the half-brother. His wife Fanny talks him out of helping his sisters.
  14. Willoughby's secret
    He seduced and abandoned Eliza, Colonel Brandon's ward. He marries rich Miss Grey.
  15. Who does Lucy Steele end up marrying?
    Robert Ferrars, Edward's brother, who got the inheritance.
  16. Free indirect discourse
    Narration that slips into a character's thoughts without quotation marks. Austen's signature.
  17. Jane Eyre pseudonym and subtitle
    ‘Currer Bell’; An Autobiography.
  18. The red-room
    Where Jane's uncle died; Jane is locked in, panics and faints. Imprisonment and anger.
  19. Mr Brocklehurst
    Hypocritical Evangelical who runs Lowood.
  20. Helen Burns
    Jane's friend at Lowood; Christian endurance; dies of consumption.
  21. Bertha Mason
    Rochester's first wife, a Creole from Jamaica, locked in the attic at Thornfield.
  22. What splits after Rochester's proposal?
    The chestnut tree, struck by lightning.
  23. How much does Jane inherit, and what does she do?
    £20,000; she splits it equally with her three cousins.
  24. St John Rivers
    Cold missionary cousin who wants Jane as a wife for India, without love.
  25. How does Thornfield end?
    Bertha burns it and jumps from the roof; Rochester is blinded and loses a hand.
  26. Gilbert & Gubar
    The Madwoman in the Attic (1979): Bertha as Jane's dark double, her repressed rage.
  27. Wide Sargasso Sea
    Jean Rhys (1966): Bertha's story from her side (Antoinette). Postcolonial rewriting.
  28. Coketown
    Fictional northern mill town in Hard Times, partly modelled on Preston.
  29. Hard Times: the three books
    Sowing, Reaping, Garnering.
  30. ‘Girl number twenty’
    Sissy Jupe, who can't define a horse.
  31. Bitzer
    Model Utilitarian pupil; defines a horse; pure self-interest.
  32. Bounderby's lie
    Claims he was abandoned in a ditch; actually raised by his loving mother, Mrs Pegler.
  33. Stephen Blackpool
    Honest weaver; trapped in marriage; refuses to join the union; framed; dies in the Old Hell Shaft. ‘It's aw a muddle.’
  34. Who robs the bank in Hard Times?
    Tom Gradgrind, ‘the whelp’, who frames Stephen.
  35. ‘Hands’
    Dickens' metonymy for factory workers: people reduced to body parts.
  36. Slackbridge
    Loud union agitator; Dickens' distrust of unions.
  37. “The Cry of the Children”: inspiration
    R. H. Horne's report for the Children's Employment Commission (1842–43).
  38. EBB poem: epigraph
    From Euripides' Medea: a mother asking why her children look at her.
  39. EBB poem: main images
    Weeping children vs playing lambs and birds; the turning iron wheels; children who can't pray.
  40. A Tale of Two Cities: three books
    Recalled to Life; The Golden Thread; The Track of a Storm.
  41. Dr Manette
    Imprisoned 18 years in the Bastille (One Hundred and Five, North Tower); makes shoes.
  42. Darnay's real name
    Evrémonde.
  43. Madame Defarge's knitting
    A secret register of those to be killed.
  44. How does Carton save Darnay?
    He drugs him and takes his place at the guillotine; they look alike.
  45. Who kills Madame Defarge?
    Her own pistol goes off while fighting Miss Pross.
  46. Dickens' source for the Revolution
    Carlyle, The French Revolution (1837).
  47. Mary Barton subtitle
    A Tale of Manchester Life (1848).
  48. Who kills Harry Carson?
    John Barton, chosen by lot by the union men.
  49. How does Mary know her father is guilty?
    The gun's paper wadding is torn from a Valentine with her name on it that her father had; she finds the matching piece at home.
  50. How does Mary Barton end?
    Barton confesses, Carson forgives him, Barton dies; Mary and Jem emigrate to Canada.
  51. Esther
    Mary's aunt, a ‘fallen woman’ who tries to save Mary from repeating her fate.
  52. Engels: ‘social murder’
    Society knowingly keeps workers in deadly conditions.
  53. Engels: Manchester's layout
    Main streets lined with shops hide the working-class districts from the middle class.
  54. Gaskell vs Engels in one line
    Gaskell: Christian sympathy between classes. Engels: the system is the problem; class war.
  55. Victoria's reign
    1837–1901 (about 63 years); Lord Melbourne taught her politics.
  56. Prince Albert's death
    1861: Victoria mourned in black and withdrew for about ten years.
  57. The Great Exhibition
    1851, in the Crystal Palace: a show of British industrial power.
  58. Opium War
    1839–42: Britain wins and gets Hong Kong.
  59. Crimean War
    1853–56: Britain allied with the Ottoman Empire against Russia.
  60. Boer War
    1899–1902, South Africa: often called the first ‘total’ war.
  61. Empress of India
    Victoria, from 1876 (Crown rule of India from 1858).
  62. ‘The workshop of the world’
    Britain's nickname as the leading industrial economy.
  63. ‘Grandmother of Europe’
    Victoria: her descendants married into Europe's royal houses (Kaiser Wilhelm II was her grandson).
  64. Turnpikes
    Toll barriers that made road users pay for road repairs.
  65. Macadam and Telford
    Engineers who gave England Europe's best roads (broken-stone surfaces; roads and bridges).
  66. Watt, Volta, Cartwright
    Steam power, the battery, the textile mill.
  67. Three pillars of growth
    Coal, iron, cotton (boosted by Free Trade from 1846).
  68. The biggest social change in English history
    1750–1850: the move from countryside to towns, creating an urban proletariat.
  69. North vs South
    The industrial North against the conservative South: Gaskell's North and South.
  70. Peterloo
    1819, St Peter's Fields, Manchester: Hussars charge a crowd of 60,000; 11 killed, 400+ injured.
  71. Manchester life expectancy (her handout)
    Labourer 17, farm labourer 38; over half of labourers' children died before five.
  72. 1832 Reform Act
    Votes for men with property worth £10 a year in rent; workers excluded.
  73. The People's Charter
    Votes for all men, no property qualification for MPs; rejected 1839, 1842, 1848.
  74. Feargus O'Connor
    Chartist MP who led the 1848 Kennington Common meeting, then backed down.
  75. Why did Chartism fail? (her handout)
    Isolation from the middle class.
  76. Rotten boroughs
    Nearly empty places that still elected MPs, while new industrial cities had none.
  77. Repeal of the Corn Laws
    1846: cheaper bread; Britain admits it is industrial, not agricultural.
  78. Forster's Act
    1870: universal primary education.
  79. Trades Union Congress
    Founded 1868.
  80. Reform Acts after 1832
    1867 (Disraeli): urban workers; 1884: agricultural workers.
  81. The Bluestockings
    18th-century circle of women intellectuals led by Mrs Montagu.
  82. Mary Wollstonecraft
    A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792): education for women.
  83. ‘A good woman has no sexual desire’
    The Puritan, middle-class (Richardsonian) view that won in the 19th century.
  84. Women and the vote
    1918: women over 30; 1928: equal terms at 21 (her handout wrongly says 1939).
  85. The lower middle class
    Small traders: the most fluid class, politically unstable, often decisive in elections.
  86. Mr Osborne / Podsnap
    Satirised money-worshippers in Vanity Fair (1848) / Our Mutual Friend (1865).
  87. Lyell and Darwin
    Principles of Geology (1830–33), On the Origin of Species (1859), The Descent of Man (1871): science shakes faith.
  88. Carlyle's influence
    German thought, hero worship, an attack on laissez-faire and utilitarianism; inspired the social-problem novels of 1830–60.
  89. Dominant genre: Romantic vs Victorian
    Romantic: poetry. Victorian: the novel.
  90. Why did novel-reading boom?
    An educated middle-class reading public and circulating libraries.
  91. Vanity Fair's subtitle
    ‘A Novel without a Hero’ (Thackeray, 1848).
  92. The Tenant of Wildfell Hall
    Anne Brontë (1848): often called the first sustained feminist novel.
  93. Wuthering Heights
    Emily Brontë (1847): Gothic Romanticism from a woman's point of view.
  94. The typical Victorian novel
    Hard work, perseverance, love and luck win; virtue rewarded, wrongdoers punished; a moral lesson.
  95. Tennyson
    Poet Laureate for over 40 years; Idylls of the King; ‘The Charge of the Light Brigade’.
  96. Gaskell's pen name for Mary Barton
    ‘Cotton Mather Mills, Esq.’
  97. Reaction to Mary Barton
    Mill-owners and the Tory press furious; Carlyle praised it.
  98. North and South vs Mary Barton
    North and South is gentler: middle-class heroes, reconciliation between classes.
  99. Cranford
    Gaskell (1853): episodic sketches of genteel ladies hiding their poverty.

Victorian // Quiz

  1. The 1834 New Poor Law made relief available mainly through…
    1. cash payments
    2. workhouses
    3. churches
    4. factories
    Answer: B. Deliberately harsh, to discourage ‘idleness’.
  2. Who coined the ‘Condition of England’ question?
    1. Dickens
    2. Carlyle
    3. Mill
    4. Engels
    Answer: B. Thomas Carlyle, also behind ‘cash nexus’.
  3. In Sense and Sensibility, who represents ‘sensibility’?
    1. Elinor
    2. Lucy Steele
    3. Marianne
    4. Mrs Jennings
    Answer: C. Marianne, with her Romantic excess.

    1. Marianne
    2. Miss Grey
    3. Lucy Steele
    4. Eliza
    Answer: B. For her money.

    1. Ellis Bell

    1. Rochester
    2. Mr Brocklehurst

    1. Spivak
    2. Gilbert & Gubar
    3. Leavis
    4. Showalter

    1. London
    2. Manchester

    4. Liverpool

    1. Sissy
    2. Bitzer
    3. Tom
    4. Gradgrind
    Answer: B. Sissy, the circus girl, can't, though she knows horses.

    2. Harthouse

    1. Newgate
