How to beat this exam

  • 40% of the grade, and up to 20% off for grammar and writing mistakes (it's in the syllabus). Short, clean sentences. Proofread every answer.
  • Learning outcomes: identify, explain, compare, apply. So for every critic know: one core idea, one key term, one line, and how they differ from the one before.
  • Build the history on Abrams' four orientations (mimetic, pragmatic, expressive, objective). It turns eight names into one story the examiner can follow.
  • Expect an application question: read “The Thought-Fox” or “The Tell-Tale Heart” like a New Critic, without the author's intentions or your feelings. The two Fallacies are the trap.
  • Russian Formalism is taught Nov 4, one week before the exam. Read the notes before class.
  • Research methods are free marks: learn the MLA core elements and one Works Cited example by heart.

Theory // Intel

IResearch methods, MLA style, research ethics

The boring part that gives easy points. Know the difference between sources, how MLA cites them, and what counts as plagiarism.

Sources

  • Primary source: the literary text itself (the poem, the novel, Eliot's essay when you're studying Eliot).
  • Secondary source: writing about the primary text (criticism, theory books like Barry or Tyson).
  • A research paper needs an argument (thesis) supported by evidence from both, properly cited.

MLA (9th edition) in one screen

  • In-text citation: author + page, no comma: (Eliot 886). Two authors: (Wimsatt and Beardsley 470). Three or more: (Cain et al. 12).
  • Works Cited core elements, in order: Author. Title of source. Title of container, Other contributors, Version, Number, Publisher, Publication date, Location.
  • Example (from your own syllabus): Eliot, T. S. “Tradition and the Individual Talent.” The Norton Anthology of Theory and Criticism, edited by William E. Cain et al., 3rd ed., W. W. Norton, 2018, pp. 885–90.
  • Works Cited: alphabetical by surname, double-spaced, hanging indent. Book and journal titles in italics; essays, poems and articles in “quotation marks”.
  • Long quotations: more than four lines of prose or three lines of verse → block quotation, indented, no quotation marks.

Research ethics

  • Plagiarism: using someone's words, ideas or structure without credit. Includes patchwriting (changing a few words), self-plagiarism (reusing your old paper), and not citing a paraphrase.
  • Fabrication (inventing sources or data) and falsification (distorting them).
  • Honest attribution, accuracy, and transparency about tools (AI use counts).
What they’ll askShort-answer bait: “Write a Works Cited entry for…” or “What is the difference between a primary and secondary source?” Know the element order cold.
II–IVWhat theory is + the classical critics: Plato, Aristotle, Horace

Before anyone said “theory”, Plato attacked poetry, Aristotle defended it, and Horace told poets to teach and please. Everything after reacts to these three.

Theory vs criticism

  • Criticism: interpreting and evaluating particular works.
  • Theory: the assumptions underneath: what literature is, where meaning comes from, what criticism should do.
  • *M. H. Abrams, The Mirror and the Lamp (1953): every theory stresses one of four elements: the universe (mimetic theories), the audience (pragmatic), the artist (expressive), the work itself* (objective). Your map for the whole course.

Plato (c. 428–348 BC)

  • **Republic Books III and X: art is mimesis, an imitation of an imitation. The true bed is the Form; the carpenter's bed copies it; the painter's bed copies the carpenter's. Art is three removes from truth**.
  • Poetry feeds the emotions instead of reason and shows gods and heroes behaving badly, so it corrupts citizens. Poets are banished from the ideal republic (except hymns to the gods and praise of good men).
  • Ion: poets create through divine inspiration (a kind of madness), not knowledge or skill.
  • Abrams: mimetic theory, and hostile.

Aristotle (384–322 BC), Poetics

  • Mimesis is natural to humans and gives pleasure and learning. Art is good, not dangerous.
  • Tragedy: imitation of a serious, complete action of some magnitude, in heightened language, in dramatic (not narrative) form, arousing pity and fear to bring about catharsis.
  • Six parts: plot (the “soul” of tragedy), character, thought, diction, song, spectacle. Plot needs beginning, middle, end; unity of action.
  • Key terms: hamartia (error), peripeteia (reversal), anagnorisis (recognition).
  • Poetry is more philosophical than history: history tells what happened (particular), poetry what could happen (universal). His direct answer to Plato.

Horace (65–8 BC), Ars Poetica

  • Poetry should instruct and delight (dulce et utile). Abrams: pragmatic theory (focus on the effect on the audience).
  • Decorum: style must fit subject, genre and character.
  • Practical advice: start in medias res; keep violence offstage; five acts; revise for years before publishing.
  • Treats poetry as a craft learned by study and imitation of Greek models: the root of neoclassicism.

Ammo: lines to quote

dulce et utile
Horace, Ars Poetica · Sweet and useful: delight and instruct.
What they’ll askClassic essay: “How does Aristotle answer Plato's attack on poetry?” Mimesis as learning vs as lies; catharsis vs emotional corruption; universal vs particular.
II–IVRenaissance to Victorian: Sidney, Dryden, Pope, Wordsworth, Arnold

Five defenders of literature with five different reasons: it makes us virtuous (Sidney), it imitates human nature (Dryden), it follows Nature methodised (Pope), it expresses feeling (Wordsworth), it replaces religion (Arnold).

Sir Philip Sidney, The Defence of Poesy / An Apology for Poetry (c. 1580, pub. 1595)

  • A reply to Puritan attacks like Stephen Gosson's The School of Abuse (1579): the same anti-theatre writer from your Shakespeare course.
  • The poet is a maker (Greek poiein). Nature gives a “brazen” world; poets give a golden one.
  • The poet beats the philosopher (abstract precepts, hard to follow) and the historian (tied to particular facts) because poetry gives a “speaking picture”: example and precept together.
  • Poetry teaches, delights and moves to virtuous action.
  • Answers the charges: poets are liars? No: “he nothing affirms, and therefore never lieth.” Plato banished poets? He banished abuses, not poetry.
  • Abrams: pragmatic.

John Dryden, An Essay of Dramatic Poesy (1668)

  • A dialogue among four friends on a boat on the Thames during a naval battle with the Dutch (1665): Crites (for the ancients), Eugenius (moderns), Lisideius (French drama), Neander (English drama: Dryden's own voice).
  • Defines a play as a just and lively image of human nature, for delight and instruction.
  • Defends English drama: variety, subplots, tragicomedy, breaking the strict unities; praises Shakespeare as having the largest, most comprehensive soul.
  • Bonus link to ELIT 481: Dryden also named three kinds of translation: metaphrase, paraphrase, imitation.

Alexander Pope, An Essay on Criticism (1711)

  • A poem in heroic couplets about how to be a good critic. Pure neoclassicism.
  • Follow Nature, and the ancients' rules are Nature itself, put in order.
  • True wit is not originality: it is a familiar thought expressed better than ever before.
  • The sound should echo the sense: form imitates meaning.
  • Attacks bad critics: pride, a little learning, partial judgement, fondness for fashion.

William Wordsworth, Preface to Lyrical Ballads (1800/1802)

  • Manifesto of English Romanticism. Abrams: expressive theory (the poet's mind and feeling at the centre).
  • Good poetry is “the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings”, taking its origin from emotion recollected in tranquillity.
  • Subjects from common, rustic life; language really used by men; attack on artificial “poetic diction”.
  • The poet is a man speaking to men, with more sensibility than most.

Matthew Arnold (1822–88)

  • “The Function of Criticism at the Present Time” (1864): criticism must be disinterested (free from politics and practical aims) and try to see the object as in itself it really is; its job is to learn and spread the best that is known and thought in the world.
  • “The Study of Poetry” (1880): poetry is a criticism of life; great poetry has high seriousness; test new poems against touchstones (short lines from the great poets).
  • In an age of religious doubt, poetry will increasingly replace religion to interpret, console and sustain us.
  • Culture and Anarchy (1869): “sweetness and light”; the middle-class Philistines. Eliot's “Function of Criticism” answers Arnold's title.

Abrams' map applied

OrientationFocusCritics
MimeticArt vs the world/truthPlato, Aristotle
PragmaticEffect on the audienceHorace, Sidney, (Dryden, Pope)
ExpressiveThe artist's feelingsWordsworth
ObjectiveThe work itselfEliot (partly), New Criticism, Formalism

Ammo: lines to quote

Her world is brazen, the poets only deliver a golden.
Sidney, Defence of Poesy · Poetry improves on nature.
Now for the poet, he nothing affirms, and therefore never lieth.
Sidney · Answer to the charge that poets lie.
True wit is Nature to advantage dress'd, / What oft was thought, but ne'er so well express'd
Pope, Essay on Criticism · Neoclassical idea of originality.
The sound must seem an echo to the sense
Pope · Form fits meaning.
all good poetry is the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings
Wordsworth, Preface · Expressive theory.
to see the object as in itself it really is
Arnold · Disinterested criticism.
What they’ll askCompare questions love pairs: Sidney vs Plato (defence vs attack), Pope vs Wordsworth (rules vs feeling; poetic diction vs real language), Arnold vs Eliot (two essays on the function of criticism).
VT. S. Eliot: “Tradition and the Individual Talent” and “The Function of Criticism”

Eliot kills the Romantic genius. A poet is not a personality pouring out feelings but a catalyst inside a tradition, and criticism should look at the poem, not the poet.

Tradition and the Individual Talent (1919)

  • Tradition is not inherited automatically; it must be obtained by great labour.
  • It requires the historical sense: feeling not only the pastness of the past but its presence.
  • All existing great works form an ideal order; a really new work modifies the whole order, so past and present change each other.
  • Impersonality: the progress of an artist is a continual self-sacrifice, a continual extinction of personality. Poetry is not a turning loose of emotion but an escape from emotion.
  • The catalyst analogy: a filament of platinum makes oxygen and sulphur dioxide combine into sulphurous acid, but stays unchanged itself. The poet's mind is that catalyst: it combines feelings into something new without “expressing” itself.
  • So criticism should be directed at the poetry, not the poet. That opens the door to New Criticism.

The Function of Criticism (1923)

  • Criticism is the elucidation of works of art and the correction of taste.
  • Against critics who follow an “inner voice” (John Middleton Murry): Eliot wants outside authority, tradition, order (classicism vs romanticism).
  • The critic needs a highly developed sense of fact: comparison and analysis are the tools, not opinions.
  • The best criticism often comes from practising poets.

Related idea (not on the list, but useful)

  • Objective correlative (“Hamlet and His Problems”, 1919): emotion in art is expressed through a set of objects, a situation, or a chain of events that evokes it, not stated directly.

Eliot vs Wordsworth

WordsworthEliot
Poetry is…Overflow of powerful feelingsAn escape from emotion and personality
The poetA man speaking to men, feeling moreA catalyst, impersonal
Look atThe poet's feelingThe poem and the tradition
AbramsExpressiveMoving toward objective

Ammo: lines to quote

not a turning loose of emotion, but an escape from emotion
Eliot, Tradition and the Individual Talent · Impersonality vs Romantic expression.
a continual extinction of personality
Eliot · The poet's self-sacrifice.
What they’ll askThe obvious essay: Eliot's impersonality vs Wordsworth's spontaneous overflow. Then link Eliot forward to New Criticism (look at the poem, not the poet).
VNew Criticism: the Intentional and Affective Fallacies, applied to Hughes and Poe

The poem is a self-contained object. Don't ask what the author meant (Intentional Fallacy) and don't measure it by how it made you feel (Affective Fallacy). Read the words on the page, closely, and show how everything fits together.

The movement

  • Mainly American, 1930s–1960s: John Crowe Ransom (The New Criticism, 1941, gave the name), Cleanth Brooks (The Well Wrought Urn, 1947), Robert Penn Warren, Allen Tate, W. K. Wimsatt and Monroe Beardsley. British forerunners: I. A. Richards (practical criticism) and William Empson (Seven Types of Ambiguity).
  • The text is an autonomous object. Close reading of the words on the page.
  • Values: organic unity (every part serves the whole), tension, irony, paradox, ambiguity, resolved into unity.
  • Brooks' “heresy of paraphrase”: a poem's meaning can't be reduced to a prose summary.
  • Abrams: objective theory. Ignores biography, history, the reader.

Wimsatt & Beardsley: the two Fallacies

The Intentional Fallacy (1946)The Affective Fallacy (1949)
The mistakeJudging or interpreting a poem by the author's intentionJudging a poem by its emotional or psychological effect on readers
ConfusesThe poem with its originsThe poem with its results (what it is vs what it does)
Why wrongIntention is neither available nor desirable as a standard; the poem belongs to the public, in languageLeads to impressionism and relativism: the poem disappears
Ends inBiography and psychologySubjective feeling

Ted Hughes, “The Thought-Fox” (1957)

  • A speaker sits at midnight by a window, before a blank page, sensing something alive coming. A fox moves through the dark snowy forest, closer and closer, step by step, until it enters his head, and the page is written.
  • New Critical reading: an extended metaphor: the fox = the poem / inspiration arriving. A metapoem (a poem about writing a poem).
  • Look for: darkness/snow vs the lit room; the blank page = snow; the clock and the silence; the fox's cautious movement mirrored by enjambment and broken lines (form echoes sense); the final moment when outside and inside fuse. Unity: every image serves the fox–thought equation.
  • Exam trap: Hughes himself described it as a poem about writing. A New Critic can't use that (Intentional Fallacy): prove it from the words alone. And “it gave me chills” is the Affective Fallacy.

Edgar Allan Poe, “The Tell-Tale Heart” (1843)

  • A first-person narrator insists he is not mad while describing how he killed an old man because of his pale “vulture eye”. He watches him for seven nights, kills him on the eighth, dismembers him and hides him under the floorboards. Police arrive; he chats calmly; then he hears a beating heart growing louder and confesses.
  • New Critical reading: dramatic irony (the more he proves his sanity, the madder he sounds); unreliable narrator; repetition and dashes creating frantic rhythm; sound imagery (the heart, the watch); ambiguity (whose heart? his own?). All elements build a unified effect.
  • Again: don't explain it through Poe's life or alcoholism (Intentional/biographical), or through how scary it felt (Affective).

Ammo: lines to quote

TRUE!—nervous—very, very dreadfully nervous I had been and am; but why will you say that I am mad?
Poe, opening · The unreliable narrator's first move.
It is the beating of his hideous heart!
Poe, last line · Guilt externalised; ambiguity.
neither available nor desirable
Wimsatt & Beardsley, The Intentional Fallacy · The author's intention as a standard.
What they’ll askAlmost certain: “Read ‘The Thought-Fox’ / ‘The Tell-Tale Heart’ from a New Critical perspective.” Structure: define New Criticism and the Fallacies → close reading (images, irony, ambiguity, form) → show organic unity → note what this approach leaves out.
VIIRussian Formalism: literariness and defamiliarization

Russian critics around 1915–30 wanted a science of literature. Literature isn't special because of its ideas or feelings but because of devices that make language strange and make us see again. Taught Nov 4, a week before the exam.

Who and when

  • Moscow Linguistic Circle (1915, Roman Jakobson) and OPOJAZ (St Petersburg, 1916: Viktor Shklovsky, Boris Eichenbaum, Yuri Tynyanov). Suppressed by the Soviet state at the end of the 1920s; the ideas travelled to the Prague School and later to structuralism.
  • Called “formalists” as an insult by opponents: they cared about how literature works, not what it says about society or the author.

Key ideas

  • Literariness (literaturnost, Jakobson): the object of literary study is not literature in general but what makes a text literary: its devices, its special use of language.
  • Defamiliarization (ostranenie, Shklovsky, “Art as Technique/Device”, 1917): everyday perception becomes automatic (habitualization) and we stop seeing things. Art exists to make the stone stony: to make the familiar strange, to slow down and lengthen perception.
  • Shklovsky's example: Tolstoy describes things as if seeing them for the first time (e.g. a story told by a horse, “Kholstomer”, which makes property seem absurd).
  • Device (priem): the techniques (rhythm, metaphor, parallelism, narrative tricks) are the real content of art. “Laying bare the device”: Tristram Shandy (in ELIT 305 too) as the most typical novel because it exposes its own techniques.
  • Fabula vs syuzhet: the story's events in chronological order vs how the text arranges and presents them (plot/discourse).
  • Foregrounding (Prague School, Mukařovský): literary language stands out against normal language.
  • Propp, Morphology of the Folktale (1928): 31 fixed functions in Russian fairy tales. Bridge to structuralism.

Formalism vs New Criticism

Russian FormalismNew Criticism
Where/whenRussia, 1915–30USA/UK, 1930s–60s
GoalA science of literature: devices, literarinessInterpretation: the meaning and unity of a single text
Key ideaDefamiliarizationOrganic unity, irony, ambiguity
SharedText-centred; ignore biography and authorial feeling; focus on form
What they’ll askDefine literariness and defamiliarization, give an example, then contrast Formalism with New Criticism. You can even apply defamiliarization to “The Thought-Fox” (making thought visible as an animal).

Theory // Flashcards

Cover the answer, say it out loud, then check.

  1. Primary vs secondary source
    Primary: the literary text itself. Secondary: criticism or theory about it.
  2. MLA in-text citation
    Author and page, no comma: (Eliot 886).
  3. MLA core elements, in order
    Author. Title of source. Title of container, Other contributors, Version, Number, Publisher, Publication date, Location.
  4. MLA Works Cited layout
    Alphabetical, double-spaced, hanging indent.
  5. When do you use a block quotation in MLA?
    More than four lines of prose or three lines of verse.
  6. Patchwriting
    Copying a source's sentence structure with a few words changed: plagiarism.
  7. Abrams' four orientations
    Mimetic (world), pragmatic (audience), expressive (artist), objective (work). The Mirror and the Lamp, 1953.
  8. Plato's bed
    Form of the bed → carpenter's bed → painter's bed. Art is three removes from truth.
  9. Why does Plato banish poets?
    Poetry imitates appearances, feeds emotion over reason, and shows gods behaving badly.
  10. Plato's Ion
    Poets create by divine inspiration (madness), not knowledge.
  11. Aristotle's definition of tragedy
    Imitation of a serious, complete action of some magnitude, in heightened language, in dramatic form, through pity and fear causing catharsis.
  12. Aristotle: most important element of tragedy
    Plot (the soul of tragedy).
  13. Why is poetry more philosophical than history? (Aristotle)
    History tells particulars (what happened); poetry tells universals (what could happen).
  14. Horace's formula
    Poetry should instruct and delight (dulce et utile).
  15. Decorum (Horace)
    Style must fit subject, genre and character.
  16. In medias res
    Starting a story in the middle of the action (Horace).
  17. Who did Sidney answer?
    Stephen Gosson, The School of Abuse (1579).
  18. Sidney: poet vs philosopher vs historian
    Poet wins: joins general precept with particular example, a “speaking picture”.
  19. Sidney: do poets lie?
    No: “he nothing affirms, and therefore never lieth.”
  20. Dryden's four speakers
    Crites (ancients), Eugenius (moderns), Lisideius (French), Neander (English, Dryden's voice).
  21. Dryden's definition of a play
    A just and lively image of human nature, for delight and instruction.
  22. Pope: true wit
    What oft was thought, but ne'er so well expressed.
  23. Pope: rules
    The ancients' rules are Nature methodised: follow Nature by following them.
  24. Wordsworth's definition of poetry
    The spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings, from emotion recollected in tranquillity.
  25. Wordsworth on language
    Use language really used by men; reject artificial poetic diction.
  26. Arnold: function of criticism
    Disinterestedly learn and spread the best that is known and thought; see the object as it really is.
  27. Arnold's touchstones
    Short passages from great poets used to test other poetry.
  28. Arnold: poetry and religion
    Poetry will increasingly replace religion to interpret, console and sustain us.
  29. Eliot: tradition
    Not inherited; obtained by great labour; needs the historical sense.
  30. Eliot: the ideal order
    Existing monuments form an order that every new work modifies.
  31. Eliot: impersonality
    Poetry is an escape from emotion and personality; art as continual extinction of personality.
  32. Eliot's catalyst
    Platinum filament: combines oxygen and sulphur dioxide into sulphurous acid, unchanged itself. The poet's mind.
  33. Eliot: function of criticism
    Elucidation of works of art and the correction of taste.
  34. Objective correlative
    Objects, situation or events that evoke a particular emotion (Eliot).
  35. Who named the New Criticism?
    John Crowe Ransom, The New Criticism (1941).
  36. Organic unity
    Every part of the text contributes to one unified whole (New Criticism).
  37. Heresy of paraphrase
    Cleanth Brooks: a poem's meaning can't be reduced to a prose summary.
  38. The Intentional Fallacy
    Wimsatt & Beardsley (1946): judging a poem by the author's intention; confuses the poem with its origins.
  39. The Affective Fallacy
    Wimsatt & Beardsley (1949): judging a poem by its effect on readers; confuses what it is with what it does.
  40. “The Thought-Fox”: central metaphor
    The fox moving through snow = the poem/inspiration arriving; blank page = snow.
  41. “The Tell-Tale Heart”: key irony
    The narrator's insistence on his sanity proves his madness.
  42. Why does the narrator kill the old man?
    Because of his pale “vulture eye”.
  43. Literariness
    Jakobson: what makes a text literary, the true object of literary study.
  44. Defamiliarization
    Shklovsky: art makes the familiar strange to break automatic perception (“make the stone stony”).
  45. Habitualization
    Automatic perception that makes us stop seeing things (Shklovsky).
  46. Fabula vs syuzhet
    Events in chronological order vs how the text arranges and presents them.
  47. OPOJAZ
    St Petersburg Society for the Study of Poetic Language (1916): Shklovsky, Eichenbaum, Tynyanov.
  48. Propp
    Morphology of the Folktale (1928): 31 functions of the Russian fairy tale.

Theory // Quiz

  1. In Abrams' scheme, Wordsworth's theory is…
    1. mimetic
    2. pragmatic
    3. expressive
    4. objective
    Answer: C. The poet's feelings are at the centre.
  2. Plato says art is…
    1. more philosophical than history
    2. three removes from truth
    3. a speaking picture
    4. an escape from emotion
    Answer: B. An imitation of an imitation of the Forms.
  3. For Aristotle, the most important element of tragedy is…
    1. character
    2. spectacle
    3. plot
    4. song
    Answer: C. Plot is the soul of tragedy.
  4. “Instruct and delight” comes from…
    1. Plato
    2. Horace
    3. Pope
    4. Arnold
    Answer: B. Dulce et utile.
  5. Sidney's Defence replies to…
    1. Stephen Gosson
    2. Ben Jonson
    3. John Milton
    4. Thomas Hobbes
    Answer: A. The School of Abuse, 1579.
  6. In Dryden's Essay of Dramatic Poesy, Neander defends…
    1. the ancients
    2. French drama
    3. English drama
    4. rhyme-free tragedy only
    Answer: C. Neander speaks for Dryden.
  7. “What oft was thought, but ne'er so well expressed” defines…
    1. true wit
    2. decorum
    3. the sublime
    4. catharsis
    Answer: A. Pope, Essay on Criticism.
  8. “Emotion recollected in tranquillity” is…
    1. Arnold
    2. Eliot
    3. Wordsworth
    4. Sidney
    Answer: C. Preface to Lyrical Ballads.
  9. Arnold's “touchstones” are…
    1. rules from Aristotle
    2. short passages from great poets used to judge others
    3. moral lessons
    4. MLA guidelines
    Answer: B. From “The Study of Poetry”.
  10. Eliot compares the poet's mind to…
    1. a mirror
    2. a lamp
    3. a catalyst
    4. an Aeolian harp
    Answer: C. The platinum filament.
  11. The Intentional Fallacy confuses the poem with its…
    1. results
    2. origins
    3. readers
    4. genre
    Answer: B. The Affective Fallacy confuses it with its results.
  12. Judging a poem by how moved you were is the…
    1. Intentional Fallacy
    2. Affective Fallacy
    3. Heresy of Paraphrase
    4. Pathetic Fallacy
    Answer: B. Wimsatt & Beardsley, 1949.
  13. In “The Tell-Tale Heart”, the narrator is motivated by the old man's…
    1. money
    2. eye
    3. voice
    4. cruelty
    Answer: B. The pale “vulture eye”.
  14. Defamiliarization is associated with…
    1. Jakobson
    2. Shklovsky
    3. Propp
    4. Brooks
    Answer: B. “Art as Technique” (1917).
  15. “Literariness” as the object of study is…
    1. Jakobson
    2. Eliot
    3. Arnold
    4. Ransom
    Answer: A. Roman Jakobson.
  16. In MLA, which comes first in a Works Cited entry?
    1. Title
    2. Publisher
    3. Author
    4. Date
    Answer: C. Author. Title. Container…
  17. New Criticism's key value is…
    1. historical context
    2. authorial biography
    3. organic unity
    4. reader response
    Answer: C. Every part serves the whole.

Theory // Write

Long essay template

  1. Intro (3–4 sentences): context → the key term in the question → your thesis (an argument, not a summary).
  2. Three body paragraphs: point → evidence (short quote or precise scene) → analysis → link back to the question.
  3. Comparing two texts? Compare inside each paragraph.
  4. Conclusion: answer the question, then one wider point.
  5. 40 minutes: 5 plan, 30 write, 5 proofread.

Short-answer template

  1. Define or identify in one sentence.
  2. One specific example from a text.
  3. Why it matters.
  4. Stop at 3–5 sentences.

Who said it? Which theory?

  1. A painter's bed copies a carpenter's bed, which copies the true Bed. So the painter is far from the truth.
    Plato, Republic X (mimetic, hostile).
    • Three removes from truth.
    • Grounds for banishing poets.
    • Aristotle will answer him.
  2. Poetry is more serious and philosophical than history, because it speaks of universals.
    Aristotle, Poetics.
    • History = particular; poetry = what could happen.
    • Answer to Plato.
    • Mimetic, but positive.
  3. The best poets mix the useful with the sweet, instructing and pleasing the reader at once.
    Horace, Ars Poetica (pragmatic).
    • Dulce et utile.
    • Audience-focused.
    • Basis for Sidney and the neoclassicists.
  4. Nature's world is brass; only the poet offers a golden one. And the poet affirms nothing, so he cannot lie.
    Sidney, The Defence of Poesy.
    • Poet as maker.
    • Answer to the charge of lying.
    • Reply to Gosson.
  5. Follow Nature, and you will find the rules of the ancients are simply Nature put in order.
    Pope, An Essay on Criticism (neoclassicism).
    • Rules = Nature methodised.
    • True wit as old thoughts better expressed.
    • Contrast Wordsworth.
  6. Poetry should use the language really spoken by people and come from strong feeling, remembered in calm.
    Wordsworth, Preface to Lyrical Ballads (expressive, Romantic).
    • Spontaneous overflow.
    • Against poetic diction.
    • Contrast Eliot's impersonality.
  7. Criticism should be disinterested and spread the best that has been known and thought, seeing things as they really are.
    Arnold, “The Function of Criticism at the Present Time”.
    • Disinterestedness.
    • Culture vs Philistines.
    • Eliot answers the title in 1923.
  8. A new work alters the whole existing order of literature, and the poet's progress is a steady sacrifice of personality.
    Eliot, “Tradition and the Individual Talent”.
    • Ideal order, historical sense.
    • Impersonality, catalyst.
    • Leads to New Criticism.
  9. Asking what the poet meant is no way to judge the poem; the poem belongs to the public.
    Wimsatt & Beardsley, “The Intentional Fallacy” (New Criticism).
    • Poem vs its origins.
    • Text-centred.
    • Pair with the Affective Fallacy.
  10. To judge a poem by the tears or shivers it produces is to lose the poem in its effects.
    Wimsatt & Beardsley, “The Affective Fallacy”.
    • What it is vs what it does.
    • Impressionism and relativism.
    • Later challenged by reader-response theory.
  11. Habit swallows everything; art exists to restore the sensation of life, to make the stone feel stony.
    Shklovsky, “Art as Technique” (Russian Formalism).
    • Defamiliarization.
    • Habitualization.
    • Slowing perception.
  12. The object of literary science is not literature but what makes a given work literary.
    Jakobson (Russian Formalism).
    • Literariness.
    • A science of literature.
    • Focus on devices.

Short answers (model answers)

  1. What is the Intentional Fallacy?
    Wimsatt and Beardsley's term (1946) for judging or interpreting a literary work by what the author intended. They argue intention is neither available nor desirable as a standard: the poem exists in public language. It confuses the poem with its origins, turning criticism into biography.
  2. Explain Eliot's catalyst analogy.
    In “Tradition and the Individual Talent”, Eliot compares the poet's mind to a filament of platinum that makes oxygen and sulphur dioxide combine into sulphurous acid while staying unchanged itself. The poet's mind combines feelings and impressions into a new whole without expressing personality: this is his theory of impersonality.
  3. What does Sidney mean by a “speaking picture”?
    In The Defence of Poesy, Sidney says poetry is an imitation that teaches and delights, a speaking picture. Unlike philosophy (abstract precept) or history (particular facts), poetry joins the general idea with a vivid example, so it moves readers to virtue more effectively.
  4. Define defamiliarization.
    Shklovsky's concept (“Art as Technique”, 1917): habit makes our perception automatic, so we stop really seeing things. Art makes familiar objects strange (‘makes the stone stony’) by slowing down and complicating perception. Example: Tolstoy narrating through a horse.
  5. What are Abrams' four orientations?
    In The Mirror and the Lamp (1953), Abrams classifies theories by their focus: mimetic (the work's relation to the world: Plato, Aristotle), pragmatic (its effect on the audience: Horace, Sidney), expressive (the artist's feelings: Wordsworth), objective (the work itself: New Criticism).
  6. Write an MLA Works Cited entry for an essay in an anthology.
    Surname, First name. “Title of Essay.” Title of Anthology, edited by Editor Name, edition, Publisher, Year, pp. range. Example: Eliot, T. S. “Tradition and the Individual Talent.” The Norton Anthology of Theory and Criticism, edited by William E. Cain et al., 3rd ed., W. W. Norton, 2018, pp. 885–90.

Essay questions with battle plans

  1. How does Aristotle respond to Plato's attack on poetry?
    1. Thesis: Aristotle accepts Plato's idea of mimesis but reverses its value: imitation becomes a source of knowledge and controlled emotion, not corruption.
    2. Plato: three removes from truth (the bed), emotion over reason, banish the poets (Republic III, X).
    3. Aristotle: mimesis natural and educational; poetry universal, more philosophical than history.
    4. Emotion: catharsis of pity and fear vs Plato's fear of emotional excess.
    5. Form: plot, unity, probability: poetry has its own rational structure.
    6. Conclusion: the start of the debate Sidney, Arnold and others continue. Abrams: both mimetic.
  2. Compare Wordsworth's and Eliot's views of the poet and emotion.
    1. Thesis: Wordsworth puts the poet's feelings at the centre; Eliot removes personality and puts tradition and the poem at the centre.
    2. Wordsworth: spontaneous overflow, emotion recollected in tranquillity, a man speaking to men, real language.
    3. Eliot: escape from emotion, extinction of personality, catalyst, tradition and historical sense.
    4. Abrams: expressive vs (proto-)objective.
    5. Consequences: Eliot leads to New Criticism (look at the poem, not the poet).
    6. Conclusion: Romantic vs Modernist ideas of creativity.
  3. Explain the Intentional and Affective Fallacies and apply them to “The Thought-Fox” or “The Tell-Tale Heart”.
    1. Define New Criticism: autonomous text, close reading, organic unity.
    2. The two Fallacies: origins vs results; why both make the poem disappear.
    3. Application: Hughes: fox = poem, snow = page, enjambment, inside/outside fusing. Or Poe: irony, unreliable narrator, sound, ambiguity of the heart.
    4. Show the trap: what a biographical (Hughes on writing; Poe's life) or emotional reading would say, and why the New Critic rejects it.
    5. Limits: what the approach ignores (history, reader, author).
    6. Conclusion: the text-centred method and its value for close reading.
  4. Defence of literature from Sidney to Arnold: what is poetry for?
    1. Thesis: each critic defends literature with a different function: moral (Sidney), mimetic of human nature (Dryden), rule-based Nature (Pope), emotional truth (Wordsworth), cultural-religious (Arnold).
    2. Sidney: golden world, speaking picture, teach/delight/move.
    3. Dryden & Pope: neoclassical imitation of nature and rules.
    4. Wordsworth: feeling and common life.
    5. Arnold: criticism of life, touchstones, poetry replacing religion.
    6. Abrams' map to tie it together.
  5. What is defamiliarization? Compare Russian Formalism with New Criticism.
    1. Context: Russia 1915–30, OPOJAZ, a science of literature.
    2. Literariness (Jakobson) and defamiliarization (Shklovsky: habitualization, “make the stone stony”, Tolstoy's horse).
    3. Other terms: device, laying bare the device, fabula/syuzhet.
    4. Comparison: both text-centred and formal; Formalists study devices and literariness, New Critics interpret meaning and unity.
    5. Example: defamiliarization in “The Thought-Fox”.
    6. Conclusion: both against biography and emotion; Formalism leads to structuralism.
